title: Heavy Load Eccentric Calf Muscle Training for the Treatment of Chronic Achilles Tendinosis
authors: Alfredson H, Pietila T, Jonsson P, Lorentzon R
source: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
summary: Landmark RCT establishing the 12-week eccentric calf raise protocol for chronic Achilles tendinopathy. 100% of patients in the eccentric group returned to running, compared to 0% in the control group. Established pain-through-exercise as acceptable in mid-stage tendinopathy.
key_points: Eccentric heel drops performed twice daily, 3 sets of 15 repetitions for 12 weeks
Both straight-knee and bent-knee variants target gastrocnemius and soleus respectively
Pain during exercise is acceptable (up to 5/10) — this is a key departure from traditional pain-avoidance models
100% return to running vs 0% control after 12 weeks
Significant reductions in tendon thickness and neovascularisation at follow-up
Best evidence for Stage 2 loading in chronic Achilles tendinopathy
clinical_question: What is the most effective loading protocol for chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy in active patients?
applicability: Chronic (>3 months) mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy. Moderate to low irritability. Not indicated for insertional tendinopathy or acute presentations.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Two variants: straight knee (gastrocnemius) and bent knee (soleus). Perform off the edge of a step. Progress by adding load (backpack with books) when 15 reps are pain-free.

progression_criteria: Advance load (add weight) when able to complete 3x15 with pain ≤3/10. Full return to running readiness when 3x15 pain-free.
regression_criteria: Reduce to flat-ground eccentric or isometric holds if pain exceeds 5/10 consistently.
contraindications: Acute tendinopathy (<6 weeks), insertional Achilles tendinopathy, suspected partial/complete rupture, post-operative (within 12 weeks).

criteria.label: 3×15 eccentric heel drops completed with pain ≤3/10
criteria.notes: Load progression trigger: increase weight when 3×15 reps achievable at pain ≤3/10 for 2 sessions.

title: Eccentric or Concentric Exercises for the Treatment of Tendinopathies?
authors: Beyer R, Kongsgaard M, Hougs Kjær B, Øhlenschlæger T, Kjær M, Magnusson SP
source: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
summary: RCT comparing heavy slow resistance (HSR) training to Alfredson eccentric protocol. Both showed significant improvement at 12 weeks, but HSR was preferred by patients and showed greater improvements in VISA-A, patient satisfaction, and structural tendon changes. HSR matched or surpassed eccentric outcomes with higher adherence.
key_points: Heavy slow resistance: 3 sets of 15 reps (week 1-2), progressing to 4 sets of 6-8 reps (weeks 3-12)
HSR and eccentric both produced significant VISA-A improvements (27+ points)
HSR had significantly higher patient satisfaction at 12 months
Both concentric and eccentric loading components drive tendon adaptation
HSR provides more flexibility in clinical setting (gym-based, adjustable load)
Evidence base for Stage 2 HSR as equivalent or superior to pure eccentric
clinical_question: Is heavy slow resistance training more effective than isolated eccentric training for Achilles tendinopathy?
applicability: Chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, moderate to low irritability. Suitable for patients who have access to gym equipment or adjustable loading.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Begin with 3x15 (light-moderate load) weeks 1-2 for familiarisation. Progress to 4x6-8 (heavy load) by week 3. Load is prescribed to reach RPE 8/10 on last rep. Rest 2-3 minutes between sets.

progression_criteria: Increase load by ~2.5 kg when able to complete all sets with pain ≤4/10. Progress through rep range before increasing load.
regression_criteria: Reduce load if pain >5/10 during exercise or if next-day pain exceeds baseline.
contraindications: Acute presentations, high irritability, insertional tendinopathy (modify range of motion), post-surgical (12 week exclusion).

title: Isometric Exercise Induces Analgesia and Reduces Inhibition in Patellar Tendinopathy
authors: Rio E, Kidgell D, Purdam C, Gaida J, Moseley GL, Pearce AJ, Cook J
summary: Landmark study demonstrating that isometric exercise produces immediate and sustained pain relief in tendinopathy, associated with cortical inhibition changes. Isometrics produced significantly greater pain reduction (by 26 points on a 100mm VAS) than isotonic exercise immediately post-exercise. Effects sustained for 45 minutes.
key_points: Isometric exercise reduces cortical inhibition of the quadriceps — mechanism extends to Achilles tendon context
Immediate analgesic effect: significant pain reduction lasting at least 45 minutes
5 x 45-second isometric holds at 70% MVIC most effective protocol
Mechanism: descending pain inhibition via motor cortex activation
Particularly useful during high-irritability phases to maintain load without provoking symptoms
Supports use of isometrics as a primary tool in Stage 1 (Capacity Initiation)
clinical_question: Can isometric loading provide effective pain relief while maintaining tendon load in highly irritable Achilles tendinopathy?
applicability: High and moderate irritability Achilles tendinopathy. Most useful in Stage 1 (Capacity Initiation) and as a pain-management tool during competition periods.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Perform at approximately 70% of maximum voluntary isometric contraction. Wall sit or step position. Pain should be ≤3/10 during hold. Analgesic effect peaks 5-10 minutes post-exercise.

progression_criteria: Progress to slow isotonic exercises (Stage 1) when 5x45s isometric holds are consistently ≤2/10 pain. Progress to eccentric loading (Stage 2) when full isotonic loading is tolerated.
regression_criteria: Reduce hold duration or load if pain exceeds 3/10. Regress from isotonic to isometric if flare occurs.
contraindications: Suspected rupture, acute inflammatory flare with rest pain >7/10, post-surgical (seek clearance).

criteria.label: Pain during isometric calf holds ≤2/10 for 3 consecutive sessions
criteria.notes: 5×45s holds at ~70% MVIC. If pain routinely ≤2/10, tendon is ready for slow isotonic loading.

criteria.label: Next-day pain ≤3/10 consistently
criteria.notes: Elevated next-day pain indicates tendon irritability not yet settled — do not advance.

title: Validity and Reliability of the VISA-A Questionnaire for Achilles Tendinopathy
authors: Robinson JM, Cook JL, Purdam C, Visentini PJ, Ross J, Maffulli N, Taunton JE, Khan KM
summary: Original validation study of the VISA-A (Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment — Achilles) questionnaire. Established VISA-A as a valid, reliable, and responsive outcome measure for Achilles tendinopathy. Asymptomatic athletes scored 96±6; patients with chronic Achilles tendinopathy scored 64±16 at baseline.
key_points: VISA-A is an 8-item self-report questionnaire validated for Achilles tendinopathy
Maximum score = 100 (full function, no pain, full competition)
Asymptomatic athletes: mean 96 ± 6
Minimally clinically important difference (MCID) is approximately 6-13 points
High test-retest reliability (ICC > 0.93)
Sensitive to change over rehabilitation time course
Should be administered every 2-4 weeks to track progress objectively
clinical_question: How should functional outcome be objectively measured in Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation?
applicability: All stages and all irritability levels. Primary outcome measure for tracking rehabilitation progress. Administer at baseline and every 2 weeks.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Not a loading protocol — outcome measure only. Score ≥80 indicates good function. Score <40 indicates severe impairment requiring Stage 1 focus.

progression_criteria: Increase of ≥10 points over 4-week period indicates good treatment response. Score >80 supports consideration of Stage 3 loading.
regression_criteria: Decrease of >5 points indicates deterioration — review loading and consider irritability reclassification.
contraindications: None — suitable for all presentations as an outcome measure.

criteria.label: VISA-A score ≥40
criteria.notes: Score <40 indicates severe impairment; Stage 1 focus should continue.

criteria.label: VISA-A score ≥70
criteria.notes: VISA-A ≥70 required before progressing to reactive/plyometric loading.

criteria.label: VISA-A improved ≥10 points in most recent 4-week period
criteria.notes: Lack of ≥10-point improvement at 6 weeks warrants clinical review before progressing.

criteria.label: VISA-A score ≥90
criteria.notes: Asymptomatic athletes score ~96; ≥90 indicates near-full function for return to sport.

title: Is Tendon Pathology a Continuum? A Pathology Model to Explain the Clinical Presentation of Load-Induced Tendinopathy
authors: Cook JL, Purdam CR
summary: Landmark conceptual paper proposing the tendon continuum model: reactive tendinopathy → tendon disrepair → degenerative tendinopathy. Established that management differs by stage of pathology and that irritability (load sensitivity) is the key clinical modifier. Challenged the view that all tendinopathy should be treated the same way.
key_points: Tendinopathy exists on a pathological continuum, not as a discrete condition
Reactive stage: high irritability, responds to load reduction and isometrics
Disrepair stage: moderate irritability, responds to progressive loading
Degenerative stage: variable irritability, may have windows of reactivity
Irritability is the primary guide to WHAT loading dose to apply
Stage of pathology guides WHAT type of loading (isometric → isotonic → plyometric)
Pain alone is not sufficient to guide management — load response and capacity must be considered
clinical_question: How should clinicians classify and guide management of Achilles tendinopathy to account for variability in presentation and irritability?
applicability: Foundational model applicable to all stages and irritability levels. Informs the entire classification and progression framework of TenoTrainer.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Conceptual framework — not a direct loading protocol. Informs irritability-based FITT modification across all stages.

progression_criteria: Progression through continuum stages is capacity-driven, not symptom-driven. Reduced irritability enables progression of load dose, not load type.
regression_criteria: Return to earlier stage loading type (e.g., reactive tendinopathy from overload) warrants temporary shift to isometrics and irritability management.
contraindications: N/A — conceptual framework.

title: Strength Classification and Diagnosis: Not All Strength Is Created Equal
authors: James LP, Talpey SW, Young WB, Geneau MC, Newton RU, Gastin PB
source: Strength and Conditioning Journal, Vol. 45, No. 3, NSCA
summary: Contemporary evidence-based framework reducing the many strength and speed-strength metrics into 5 empirically distinct qualities: (1) maximal isometric strength, (2) explosive strength, (3) heavy maximal dynamic strength, (4) fast maximal dynamic strength, and (5) reactive strength. Each quality has limited commonality (r² < 0.50) with the others, meaning they must be assessed and trained independently. The framework has direct application to Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation staging, where each rehab stage targets a different strength quality on this continuum.
key_points: Five distinct strength qualities exist: maximal isometric, explosive, heavy dynamic, fast dynamic, and reactive — each requires specific assessment and targeted training
Maximal isometric strength (IMTP/isometric squat peak force) maps directly to Stage 1 Achilles rehab — isometric loading builds foundational tendon capacity
Heavy maximal dynamic strength (1RM/HSR, 3-1-3 tempo) maps to Stage 2 — eccentric and concentric loading drives tendon structural adaptation
Reactive strength (drop jump RSI, contact time <0.25 s) maps to Stage 3 — plyometric and elastic loading restores tendon energy storage and release function
Shares only 10–35% commonality with other strength qualities, confirming that Stage 3 readiness cannot be inferred from Stage 2 performance alone
Stronger athletes (≥2.0× BM back squat) respond better to high-velocity and plyometric training — chronic load base must be established first
Reactive strength index (RSI) = jump height ÷ contact time — primary metric for Stage 3 readiness and plyometric progression
Fast movement time in a slow SSC task (e.g., CMJ) does NOT imply fast contact time in reactive strength — separate assessment is required
Training should be periodized and sequenced: isometric → heavy dynamic → fast dynamic → reactive strength, mirroring the 3-stage rehab model
Weaker or less-trained individuals improve broadly from heavy strength training; more specific targeting is required as strength improves
clinical_question: How should strength qualities be classified, assessed, and sequenced to guide progression through Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation stages?
applicability: Applicable across all stages of Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation. Provides the theoretical and evidence base for why each rehab stage targets a different strength quality and why stage progression requires capacity assessment, not pain response alone. Particularly relevant to Stage 2→3 transition and return-to-sport readiness.

stage_1_isometric.notes: Assess peak force to establish baseline. 'Hard and fast' cue for maximal output.

stage_2_heavy_dynamic.type: Heavy maximal dynamic strength — calf raises with load
stage_2_heavy_dynamic.notes: Progress load when full sets completed with pain ≤3/10. Velocity at ≥80% 1RM load is a valid proxy when RM testing is not feasible.

stage_3_reactive.type: Reactive strength — single-leg hops, drop jumps
stage_3_reactive.notes: Bilateral before unilateral. Aim for 200–250 contacts per session when building running readiness. Do not infer Stage 3 readiness from Stage 2 performance — assess separately.

progression_criteria: Progress from Stage 1 to Stage 2 when isometric holds are consistently ≤2/10 pain and functional calf raise capacity is improving. Progress from Stage 2 to Stage 3 when heavy dynamic loading (4x6-8 at RPE 8) is well tolerated AND reactive strength has been formally assessed (RSI via drop jump or hop test). Do not progress based on pain alone.
regression_criteria: If reactive strength testing reveals deficiency relative to heavy dynamic strength (large gap between Stage 2 and Stage 3 performance), do not attempt Stage 3 loading — consolidate Stage 2 and introduce bilateral slow-SSC plyometrics as a bridge.
contraindications: Stage 3 reactive/plyometric loading is contraindicated until Stage 2 heavy dynamic capacity is well established (minimum 4 consistent weeks). Return to sport is NOT automated — clinician decision required. High irritability precludes reactive strength loading.

criteria.label: Maximal isometric calf strength improving over 3+ consecutive sessions
criteria.notes: Full isometric session compliance (sets ≥90%) for 3 sessions indicates adequate Stage 1 capacity.

criteria.label: Heavy slow resistance (4×6-8 reps at RPE 8) completed with pain ≤4/10
criteria.notes: Stage 2 HSR at RPE 8 must be well tolerated for ≥4 sessions before Stage 3 reactive loading.

criteria.label: Reactive strength formally assessed (drop jump RSI or hop test)
criteria.notes: Do not infer Stage 3 readiness from Stage 2 performance alone — reactive strength must be directly assessed.

criteria.label: Minimum 4 consistent weeks at current Stage 2 load
criteria.notes: At 3×/week, 12 sessions = 4 weeks of established chronic workload before reactive loading is safe.

title: The Training-Injury Prevention Paradox: Should Athletes Train Smarter and Harder?
authors: Gabbett TJ
summary: Highly cited paper establishing the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) as a predictor of injury risk. Demonstrates that well-prepared athletes (high chronic workload) tolerate spikes better, and that sudden load increases are the primary injury risk — not high load per se. Informs load management principles for tendon rehabilitation.
key_points: Acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) >1.5 associated with significantly elevated injury risk
High chronic workload is PROTECTIVE — fitness is a protective factor
Rapid load spikes (not high load) are the primary injury mechanism for tendons
The training-injury prevention paradox: under-training increases injury risk as much as over-training
Load monitoring should track both acute and chronic workload over rolling 1-week and 4-week windows
Conservative progression: increase total load by no more than 10% per week
Applies directly to Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation load management
clinical_question: How should load be progressed during Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation to minimise re-injury risk while maximising adaptation?
applicability: All stages, particularly relevant to Stage 2-3 progression and return-to-activity planning. Critical for patients with history of load spikes as a risk factor.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Load management principle: do not increase total training load by more than 10% per week. Monitor acute (1-week) vs chronic (4-week average) training load. ACWR >1.5 = high injury risk.

progression_criteria: Progress when chronic workload is well-established (≥4 consistent weeks at current load) and ACWR is 0.8–1.3.
regression_criteria: Reduce load if ACWR exceeds 1.5 or if next-day pain responses increase.
contraindications: N/A — load management principle applicable universally.

title: Which treatment is most effective for patients with Achilles tendinopathy? A living systematic review with network meta-analysis of 29 randomised controlled trials
authors: van der Vlist AC, Breda SJ, Damen PJ, Waarsing JH, Krestin GP, Verhaar JAN, de Vos RJ
summary: Living systematic review and network meta-analysis of 29 RCTs evaluating treatments for Achilles tendinopathy. Identifies wide uncertainty across treatment rankings and concludes that no single intervention is definitively superior. Reinforces that clinicians should anchor care in progressive loading protocols rather than chasing small between-intervention differences. Highest-evidence comparative synthesis for Achilles tendinopathy treatment effectiveness.
key_points: Living NMA of 29 RCTs — highest-level synthesis for Achilles tendinopathy treatment comparison
Wide confidence intervals across treatment rankings indicate substantial uncertainty
Exercise-based loading is consistently in the top-performing cluster across analyses
Adjuncts (e.g., injections, shockwave) show inconsistent benefit and should not replace loading
Clinical decisions should be grounded in progressive loading, adherence, and symptom-guided progression
Risk of bias is substantial across included trials, limiting certainty of rankings
Directly practice-shaping for evidence-based rehabilitation program design
clinical_question: Which treatment approach is most effective for Achilles tendinopathy across all available RCT evidence?
applicability: All stages and irritability levels of Achilles tendinopathy. Foundational for treatment selection and evidence communication with patients.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Synthesis paper — not a direct loading protocol. Supports progressive loading as the cornerstone intervention across treatment comparisons.

progression_criteria: Use loading-based progression criteria from stage-specific protocols (see kb_001, kb_002, kb_003). No single adjunct warrants deviation from progressive loading.
regression_criteria: Regression decisions should follow irritability classification (see kb_005), not absence of adjunct response.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review. Individual study contraindications apply to specific interventions.

title: Efficacy of heel lifts versus calf muscle eccentric exercise for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy (HEALTHY): a randomised trial
authors: Rabusin CL, Menz HB, McClelland JA, Tan JM, Whittaker GA, Landorf KB
summary: Pragmatic RCT comparing heel lifts (passive offloading) versus the Alfredson eccentric calf raise protocol for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy. Both groups improved significantly over 12 weeks, but eccentric exercise demonstrated superior VISA-A improvements at 12 weeks. Heel lifts may provide a useful short-term adjunct but should not replace progressive loading.
key_points: Eccentric exercise (Alfredson protocol) produced superior VISA-A improvement vs heel lifts at 12 weeks
Both groups improved significantly — heel lifts are not ineffective, but inferior as standalone treatment
Heel lifts may reduce acute Achilles load and provide short-term symptom relief
Pragmatic design supports real-world applicability in clinical and community settings
Reinforces eccentric loading as the standard non-surgical intervention for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy
Patient-reported outcomes (VISA-A) used as primary endpoint — clinically meaningful
clinical_question: Are heel lifts an effective alternative or adjunct to eccentric exercise for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy?
applicability: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, moderate to low irritability. Heel lifts may support early symptom management but eccentric loading should remain the primary intervention.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Alfredson eccentric protocol as per kb_001. Heel lifts (full-length, 12–15mm) may be used as adjunct in early symptomatic phase. Remove heel lifts as loading capacity improves.

progression_criteria: Progress eccentric load when 3x15 reps pain ≤3/10. Wean heel lifts when pain at rest and morning stiffness are consistently low.
regression_criteria: Reintroduce heel lifts temporarily if pain spikes with activity. Reduce eccentric load if pain >5/10.
contraindications: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (heel lifts may worsen insertion compression). Acute presentations.

title: Rate of Improvement of Pain and Function in Mid-Portion Achilles Tendinopathy with Loading Protocols: A Systematic Review and Longitudinal Meta-Analysis
authors: Murphy M, Travers M, Gibson W, Chivers P, Debenham J, Docking S, Rio E
summary: Systematic review and longitudinal meta-analysis quantifying the time-course of pain and function improvements with loading protocols in mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy. Demonstrates meaningful, progressive improvements in VISA-A over weeks 0–12, providing clinicians with evidence-based prognosis benchmarks. Key for expectation-setting and trial design in tendinopathy rehabilitation.
key_points: Significant VISA-A improvements occur across weeks 0–12 with loading protocols
Greatest rate of improvement typically occurs in the first 6 weeks
Continued (slower) improvement occurs between weeks 6–12 and beyond
Longitudinal meta-analysis design captures trajectory rather than just endpoint — valuable for prognostication
Supports patient expectation-setting: meaningful gains are achievable in 6–12 weeks
Loading type (eccentric, HSR, isometric) does not significantly alter the improvement trajectory
Adherence to loading protocol is a stronger predictor of outcome than loading type
clinical_question: What is the expected rate and trajectory of improvement in pain and function with loading protocols for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy?
applicability: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, all irritability levels. Particularly useful for patient counselling, setting realistic milestones, and monitoring treatment response.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Synthesis paper — not a direct loading protocol. Supports 12-week minimum commitment to loading programs. Benchmark: expect VISA-A improvement of 15–25 points at 6 weeks, 25–35 points at 12 weeks.

progression_criteria: Use VISA-A trajectory as a progression benchmark. Lack of ≥10-point improvement at 6 weeks warrants clinical review of loading dose and adherence.
regression_criteria: Deterioration in VISA-A over 2+ consecutive assessments indicates over-loading or irritability reclassification needed.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review.

title: Nonoperative or Surgical Treatment of Acute Achilles' Tendon Rupture
authors: Myhrvold SB, Brouwer EF, Andresen TKM, Rydevik K, Amundsen M, Grün W, Ulstein S, Nilsen F, Figved W, Finished W, Engebretsen L
summary: Landmark multicenter RCT comparing operative versus nonoperative management of acute Achilles tendon rupture. Found no significant difference in patient-important outcomes (Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score) between groups when both received modern rehabilitation protocols. Surgical group had higher complication rates. Supports shared decision-making with emphasis on modern rehabilitation over automatic surgical referral.
key_points: No significant difference in primary outcome (ATRS) between operative and nonoperative groups at 12 months
Operative group had significantly higher complication rates (wound infection, nerve damage)
Modern early functional rehabilitation protocol is key — both groups received structured rehab
Re-rupture rates were similar between groups in this well-controlled RCT
Challenges historical assumption that surgery is superior for active patients
Shared decision-making should weigh patient preference, activity level, and complication risk
Published in NEJM — highest-impact venue; informs international clinical guidelines
clinical_question: Is surgical repair of acute Achilles tendon rupture superior to nonoperative management with modern rehabilitation?
applicability: Acute Achilles tendon rupture. Informs shared decision-making regarding operative vs nonoperative pathways and rehabilitation planning post-rupture.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: RCT — not a loading protocol. Both groups received early functional rehabilitation (weight-bearing within 2 weeks, progressive loading). Modern rehab protocol is the critical variable, not surgical vs nonoperative.

progression_criteria: Early weight-bearing within 1–2 weeks regardless of operative status. Progressive loading milestones: full weight-bearing by week 6, return to jogging ~3–4 months, return to sport ~6–9 months.
regression_criteria: Pain >6/10 or re-rupture symptoms (sudden sharp pain, palpable gap) require immediate clinical reassessment.
contraindications: Operative: active infection, vascular compromise, severe skin condition at site. Nonoperative: patient preference for surgery after counselling is respected.

title: Early functional rehabilitation versus traditional immobilization for surgical Achilles tendon repair after acute rupture: a systematic review of overlapping meta-analyses
authors: Zhao JG, Yu XW, Zhao J, Liang GB
summary: Systematic review consolidating overlapping and sometimes discordant meta-analyses on early functional rehabilitation versus traditional immobilization after surgical Achilles tendon repair. Concludes that early functional rehabilitation does not increase re-rupture rates and significantly improves return-to-activity outcomes. Supports early weight-bearing and functional protocols post-surgical repair.
key_points: Early functional rehabilitation is safe — no increase in re-rupture rates vs immobilization
Early functional rehab improves return-to-activity speed and patient satisfaction
Addresses discordance between prior meta-analyses using a systematic overlap approach
Open-access (PMC) — widely accessible for clinical teams
Directly informs post-surgical Achilles rehabilitation pathways
Traditional cast immobilization is not superior and delays recovery
Supports immediate post-operative mobilization protocols
clinical_question: Should early functional rehabilitation replace traditional immobilization after surgical Achilles tendon repair?
applicability: Post-surgical acute Achilles tendon rupture. Informs immediate post-operative rehabilitation protocol design.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Synthesis paper — not a direct protocol. Supports early weight-bearing (within 2 weeks post-op) and functional rehabilitation over cast immobilization.

progression_criteria: Early weight-bearing in a boot within 1–2 weeks. Transition to full weight-bearing by weeks 4–6. Progressive strengthening from week 6 onwards.
regression_criteria: Increased wound pain, swelling, or wound breakdown warrants temporary load reduction and surgical team review.
contraindications: Wound complications, active infection, non-compliance with weight-bearing guidelines.

title: Resistance training prescription for muscle strength and hypertrophy: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
authors: Currier BS, Mcleod JC, Banfield L, Beyene J, Welton NJ, D'Souza AC, Oikawa SY, Wang X, Philpott JD, Bretz F, Thabane L, Phillips SM
summary: High-impact Bayesian network meta-analysis integrating multiple resistance training prescription variables (load, volume, frequency, rest) for strength and hypertrophy. Improves practical translation beyond single-variable analyses by simultaneously modelling prescription interactions. One of the most comprehensive contemporary summaries of resistance training dose-response relationships for clinical and coaching application.
key_points: Bayesian NMA approach enables simultaneous comparison of multiple prescription variables — superior to pairwise MA
Higher loads (≥60% 1RM) favour maximal strength gains; hypertrophy is achievable across a wide load spectrum
Volume (sets per muscle per week) is a primary driver of hypertrophy dose-response
Frequency effects are largely mediated by total volume — equating volume attenuates frequency differences
Failure proximity (training to or near failure) is important for hypertrophy, especially at lower loads
Directly informs Stage 2 prescription parameters for Achilles rehabilitation (load, volume, rest)
198 citations — rapidly becoming the definitive modern synthesis for resistance training prescription
clinical_question: What resistance training prescription variables (load, volume, frequency) optimise strength and hypertrophy outcomes?
applicability: Applicable to all stages of Achilles rehabilitation requiring progressive resistance loading (Stage 2 primary). Informs clinical prescription of calf raise loading parameters.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: For strength: prioritise ≥75% 1RM equivalent, lower reps (6-8). For hypertrophy/tendon adaptation: moderate loads (60-75% 1RM), moderate reps (10-15), train close to failure. Rest 2-3 min between sets.

progression_criteria: Increase load by ~2.5–5 kg when all sets completed with RPE ≤8/10. Progress rep range before increasing load for hypertrophy focus.
regression_criteria: Reduce load or volume if next-day pain exceeds baseline or VISA-A declines.
contraindications: High irritability phases — reduce to isometric or low-load isotonic (see kb_003). Post-surgical within 6 weeks.

title: Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis
authors: Lopez P, Radaelli R, Taaffe DR, Newton RU, Galvão DA, Trajano GS, Teodoro JL, Kraemer WJ, Häkkinen K, Pinto RS
summary: Seminal network meta-analysis clarifying load-specificity for hypertrophy and strength outcomes in resistance training. Demonstrates that strength gains significantly favour heavier loads, while hypertrophy can be achieved across a broad load range when sets are taken to volitional failure. One of the most highly cited (434 citations) modern resistance training meta-analyses.
key_points: Maximal strength gains are load-specific — heavier loads (≥70% 1RM) produce superior 1RM improvements
Muscle hypertrophy is largely load-independent when sets are taken to volitional failure
Low-load training to failure is a viable hypertrophy strategy for tendon rehab contexts (reduces compressive stress)
Network approach enables indirect comparisons across load ranges not directly compared in primary RCTs
434 citations — among the most influential modern resistance training syntheses
Directly informs Stage 2 load selection: heavy loads for strength; moderate loads acceptable for tissue hypertrophy
Failure proximity matters more than load for hypertrophy — important for clinical load prescription
clinical_question: Does training load (light vs heavy) differentially affect muscle hypertrophy and maximal strength gains?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation and return to performance. Informs when to prioritise heavier loading (strength goals) vs moderate loading to failure (hypertrophy/tendon adaptation).

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Strength target: ≥70% 1RM, 6-8 reps. Hypertrophy target: 40-70% 1RM to near-failure, 10-15 reps. Both valid for tendon adaptation; choose based on clinical goal and irritability.

progression_criteria: Increase load when full prescribed reps are completed with RPE <8. For strength: prioritise load increases. For hypertrophy: prioritise training close to failure before increasing load.
regression_criteria: Reduce to lower loads or isometrics if pain >5/10 during loading.
contraindications: High irritability — avoid heavy maximal loading until irritability reduces.

title: Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations Between Low- vs. High-Load Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
source: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
summary: Landmark systematic review and meta-analysis (1212 citations) examining hypertrophy and strength adaptations across low-load and high-load resistance training. Established the foundational position that hypertrophy is similar across load ranges when volume is equated and effort is sufficient, while strength gains favour heavier loads. Highly influential in shaping modern load-selection practice.
key_points: Hypertrophy is similar between low-load and high-load training when volume is equated
Maximal strength (1RM) significantly favours high-load training (specificity principle)
1212 citations — one of the most foundational resistance training meta-analyses of the decade
Challenges earlier dogma that heavy loads are required for muscle growth
Practical implication: use heavier loads for strength-focused rehab stages; moderate loads are viable for hypertrophy
Applicable to calf raise prescription in Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation
Volume-equating is a critical methodological consideration when comparing load conditions
clinical_question: Is heavy loading necessary for muscle hypertrophy, or can lower loads achieve equivalent adaptations?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation. Justifies use of moderate loading protocols when heavy loads are not tolerated, without compromising hypertrophy targets.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: For hypertrophy equivalence: moderate loads (50-70% 1RM) to near-failure are sufficient. For maximal strength: ≥75% 1RM required. Effort (proximity to failure) matters more than absolute load for hypertrophy.

progression_criteria: Progress load when reps are completed with good form and RPE <8. Volume is the primary driver — add sets before adding load for hypertrophy.
regression_criteria: Reduce load if pain >4/10 or technique breaks down.
contraindications: High irritability. Avoid any loading that provokes pain >5/10 during exercise.

title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
summary: Highly cited systematic review and meta-analysis (1047 citations) establishing a positive dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume (sets per muscle group per week) and muscle hypertrophy. Demonstrates that higher weekly set volumes produce greater muscle mass increases, up to a practical ceiling. Foundational for volume periodization in both athletic and rehabilitation contexts.
key_points: Positive dose-response between weekly sets per muscle group and hypertrophy
≥10 sets per muscle per week produces greater hypertrophy than lower volumes
Volume is a primary programming lever for muscle mass — not just load or frequency
1047 citations — among the most influential sports science papers of its era
Practical upper limit exists (high volume also increases recovery demand)
Supports progressive volume overload as a primary mechanism for tendon tissue remodelling
Informs Phase 2 loading progression: increase sets before increasing load
clinical_question: How does weekly resistance training volume (number of sets) affect muscle hypertrophy outcomes?
applicability: Stage 2 and Stage 3 Achilles rehabilitation. Informs how to progress loading volume over the 12-week rehabilitation programme.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Begin at lower weekly volume (6-8 sets/week for calf group) and build to 10-15 sets/week over 4-6 weeks. Do not increase load and volume simultaneously — prioritise one variable at a time.

progression_criteria: Add 1-2 sets per week every 2 weeks when current volume is well tolerated. Monitor next-day pain response as volume proxy.
regression_criteria: Reduce weekly volume by 20-30% if next-day pain increases or VISA-A declines.
contraindications: High irritability. Avoid volume progression during reactive tendinopathy phase.

title: Effect of resistance training frequency on gains in muscular strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Grgic J, Schoenfeld BJ, Davies TB, Lazinica B, Krieger JW, Pedisic Z
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (618 citations) examining how resistance training frequency affects maximal strength gains. Finds that higher training frequencies produce greater strength gains when volume is not equated, but the effect attenuates substantially when total volume is matched. Context-dependent: training status, volume distribution, and programme design moderate frequency effects.
key_points: Higher training frequency generally produces greater strength gains when volume is not equated
When volume is equated, frequency effects on strength are substantially reduced
Trained individuals may benefit more from higher frequencies than beginners
618 citations — highly influential for programming frequency decisions
Practical implication: 2-3x/week is sufficient for rehab strength gains when volume is managed
Frequency manipulations should be used to distribute volume, not replace volume
Directly relevant to scheduling exercise sessions in Achilles rehabilitation microcycles
clinical_question: How does resistance training frequency affect strength gains, and what is the optimal frequency for rehabilitation?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation. Informs session frequency prescription (typically 3x/week for HSR protocols).

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: 3x/week is standard for Stage 2 rehabilitation. Higher frequency (4-5x/week) is not meaningfully superior when total volume is matched. Allow 48h between sessions for tendon recovery.

progression_criteria: Maintain 3x/week as standard. Increase frequency only when total volume per session cannot be further increased.
regression_criteria: Reduce to 2x/week during high-volume weeks or when fatigue accumulates.
contraindications: Daily training of the same tendon group is not recommended during active rehabilitation phases.

title: The effects of plyometric jump training on physical fitness attributes in basketball players: A meta-analysis
authors: Ramirez-Campillo R, Moran J, Chaabene H, Granacher U, Garcia-Hermoso A, Behm D, Negra Y, Scanlan AT
source: Journal of Sport and Health Science
summary: Large meta-analysis of plyometric jump training (PJT) in basketball players demonstrating consistent improvements in jumping, sprinting, and change-of-direction performance. Identifies dose and program design moderators. Provides clear performance benchmarks and dose recommendations directly applicable to Stage 3 Achilles rehabilitation and return-to-sport plyometric programming.
key_points: PJT produces significant improvements in jump height, sprint speed, and change-of-direction in basketball players
255 citations — highly influential in sport-specific plyometric programming literature
Training dose (volume, intensity, duration) moderates effect magnitude
Progressive PJT over 6-10 weeks produces the largest performance benefits
Bilateral exercises before unilateral — essential sequencing principle for Achilles rehab
Directly applicable to Stage 3 Achilles rehabilitation plyometric progression
Supports minimum 200-250 contacts per session as a volume target for tendon loading
clinical_question: What is the evidence for plyometric training effectiveness and optimal dose for athletic performance in jump-based sports?
applicability: Stage 3 Achilles rehabilitation and return-to-sport. Informs plyometric progression structure, volume targets, and readiness benchmarks for sport-specific loading.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Progress bilateral → unilateral. Start: 50-80 contacts/session. Build to 200-250 contacts/session over 6-8 weeks. Prioritise quality (maximal intent, fast ground contact) over quantity. RSI target >1.5 for sport readiness.

progression_criteria: Advance from bilateral to unilateral when bilateral drop jump RSI >1.2 and pain ≤2/10. Progress contact volume by 20-30 contacts/session per week.
regression_criteria: Return to bilateral loading if unilateral pain >3/10 or technique deteriorates. Reduce volume by 30% if next-day pain exceeds baseline.
contraindications: Stage 1 or high irritability. Plyometric loading contraindicated until Stage 2 heavy dynamic loading is well established (minimum 4 weeks).

title: Plyometric-jump training effects on physical fitness and sport-specific performance according to maturity: A systematic review with meta-analysis
authors: Ramirez-Campillo R, Moran J, Oliver JL, Taber CB, Hughes MG, Reyes A, Lloyd RS
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis examining the effects of plyometric jump training across maturity levels in youth athletes. Demonstrates that PJT is effective both pre- and post-peak height velocity, with maturity status shaping expected magnitude of gains. Provides dose recommendations for youth populations and supports age-appropriate plyometric programming in rehabilitation contexts.
key_points: PJT is effective for physical fitness and sport-specific performance across maturity stages
Both pre- and post-PHV athletes benefit, though effect sizes differ by maturity status
Maturity-appropriate dose and exercise selection improve safety and efficacy in youth
Open-access publication — widely accessible for clinicians working with youth athletes
Directly applicable for paediatric Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation Stage 3 planning
Supports minimum effective dose programming for injury prevention in youth sport
107 citations — rapidly growing evidence base for maturity-stratified plyometric programming
clinical_question: Is plyometric jump training safe and effective for youth athletes, and does maturity status affect response?
applicability: Stage 3 Achilles rehabilitation in adolescent/youth patients. Informs age-appropriate plyometric dose and exercise selection based on maturity status.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Pre-PHV: lower volume (60-100 contacts/session), bilateral, submaximal. Post-PHV: can progress to adult-level volumes. Prioritise landing mechanics before increasing intensity. Supervise closely during growth spurts.

progression_criteria: Advance from submaximal to maximal intent when landing mechanics are consistently safe. Progress bilateral → unilateral. Increase volume by 10-15 contacts/session weekly.
regression_criteria: Reduce to submaximal bilateral if pain emerges or technique degrades. Reassess maturity status during rapid growth phases.
contraindications: Active growth plate stress, acute tendon pain >4/10. Consult paediatric sports medicine if growth plate injury is suspected.

title: Strength training vs. plyometric training on physical performance in female soccer players: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Pardos-Mainer E, Casajus JA, Gonzalez-Aguero A, Bishop C, Colomer-Poveda D, Marcos-Frutos D, Gallego-Izquierdo T, Jimenez-Gutierrez A, Serrano-Ostarez E
source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
summary: Highly cited meta-analysis comparing strength training and plyometric training effects on physical performance in female soccer players. Both modalities improve performance, with plyometrics showing advantages for explosive performance. Addresses a population (female athletes) underrepresented in older plyometric literature. Directly supports sex-specific consideration in Stage 3 programming.
key_points: Both strength and plyometric training improve physical performance in female soccer players
Plyometrics show greater advantages for explosive outcomes (jumping, sprint acceleration)
Strength training shows advantages for maximal strength and deceleration capacity
Female athletes require specific consideration — response may differ from male-dominant literature
173 citations — highest-cited comparator meta-analysis for strength vs plyometrics in female sport
Supports combined strength + plyometric programming for comprehensive Stage 3 preparation
Informs sex-specific programming in return-to-sport Achilles rehabilitation
clinical_question: Is strength training or plyometric training more effective for physical performance in female athletes?
applicability: Stage 3 Achilles rehabilitation in female athletes. Supports combined strength and plyometric programming for comprehensive return-to-sport preparation.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Combine strength (HSR calf raises) and plyometric training (bilateral → unilateral hops) in Stage 3. For female athletes, ensure adequate strength base before advancing to high-intensity plyometrics.

progression_criteria: Advance plyometric intensity when maximal strength (HSR 4x6-8) is well established. Add reactive strength work when bilateral plyometrics are pain-free.
regression_criteria: Prioritise strength consolidation if plyometric load causes pain escalation.
contraindications: Insufficient Stage 2 strength base. Plyometrics without established heavy dynamic strength capacity.

title: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Plyometric-Jump Training in Combat Sport Athletes
authors: Ojeda-Aravena A, Herrera-Valenzuela T, Valdés-Badilla P, Cancino-López J, Tuesta M, Ramírez-Campillo R
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis extending plyometric jump training evidence to combat sport athletes. Demonstrates broad applicability of PJT principles across diverse sport populations beyond field/court sports. Confirms consistent performance improvements and supports generalisation of plyometric programming principles across sport contexts.
key_points: PJT produces significant performance improvements in combat sport athletes
Generalises plyometric programming principles beyond field and court sports
Supports PJT as a universal Stage 3 tool applicable across sport types
Open-access publication (PMC)
Effect sizes comparable to field sport literature — confirms generalisability
Programme design factors (volume, frequency, duration) remain primary moderators
58 citations — growing evidence base for sport-specific plyometric programming
clinical_question: Is plyometric training effective for athletic performance across diverse sport populations beyond field sports?
applicability: Stage 3 Achilles rehabilitation. Supports plyometric programming for patients returning to non-field sports (combat sports, court sports, general athleticism).

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Standard PJT principles apply across sport types. Adjust exercise selection to match sport-specific demands (lateral movements, deceleration, rotational loading as appropriate).

progression_criteria: Progress exercise specificity towards sport demands as pain and capacity allow. Add lateral and deceleration plyometrics after sagittal plane competence is established.
regression_criteria: Reduce specificity and intensity if pain >3/10 or fatigue accumulates.
contraindications: Insufficient Stage 2 capacity. High-irritability phase.

title: Effects of plyometric training on health-related physical fitness: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Deng N, Soh KG, Abdullah BB, Huang B
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrating plyometric training effects extend beyond sport performance to health-related physical fitness domains including cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and musculoskeletal health. Broadens the clinical application of plyometric programming to general conditioning and injury prevention contexts beyond elite sport.
key_points: PJT improves health-related physical fitness across multiple domains
Benefits include improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle strength, and body composition
Applicable to non-elite populations for prevention and general conditioning
Open-access publication (Scientific Reports)
Supports plyometric training as a general health intervention, not only performance-focused
Particularly relevant for general-population Achilles tendinopathy patients returning to recreational activity
33 citations — newer but growing evidence base
clinical_question: Can plyometric training improve health-related fitness outcomes in non-elite or general populations?
applicability: Stage 3 Achilles rehabilitation for recreational and general-population patients. Supports plyometric programming beyond sport-specific contexts.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: For recreational patients: begin with low-impact bilateral jumps (jump squats, skipping), progress to single-leg hops. Lower volume targets (100-150 contacts/session) appropriate for non-athletes.

progression_criteria: Advance contact intensity when bilateral competence and pain control are established. Goal for recreational patients: pain-free single-leg hop and return to activity-specific demands.
regression_criteria: Reduce intensity and volume if next-day pain increases or function declines.
contraindications: High irritability, Stage 1 phase, insufficient Stage 2 strength base.

title: Determining the Sites of Neural Adaptations to Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
authors: Siddique U, Rahman S, Frazer AK, Pearce AJ, Howatson G, Kidgell DJ
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis explicitly mapping where neural adaptations to resistance training occur within the CNS — cortical, subcortical, and spinal sites. Identifies reduced intracortical inhibition and altered corticospinal excitability as key early neural signatures of strength training. Provides mechanistic foundation for understanding why early strength gains precede structural muscle changes.
key_points: Neural adaptations occur at multiple sites: cortical (M1), subcortical, and spinal levels
Reduced intracortical inhibition is a dominant early neural signature of strength training
Neural adaptations precede structural (hypertrophy) adaptations — explain early strength gains in rehab
174 citations — most integrative high-level CNS adaptation synthesis
Isometric training produces measurable corticospinal adaptations relevant to Stage 1 Achilles rehab
Provides mechanistic rationale for why isometric exercise produces rapid analgesia (see kb_003)
Supports sequenced neural → structural progression in rehabilitation planning
clinical_question: What are the neural mechanisms underlying early strength gains in resistance training, and where in the CNS do these adaptations occur?
applicability: All stages of Achilles rehabilitation. Provides mechanistic understanding for why isometric loading produces rapid pain relief and early strength gains. Informs expectations during Stage 1.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Mechanistic synthesis — not a direct loading protocol. Neural adaptation timeline: significant corticospinal changes within 2-4 weeks of consistent training. Supports early loading even before structural tendon changes are detectable.

progression_criteria: Neural adaptations support progression from Stage 1 to Stage 2 when pain during isometric loading is consistently ≤2/10 and functional strength is improving.
regression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework. Apply regression criteria from stage-specific protocols.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review.

title: Corticospinal responses following strength training: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Kidgell DJ, Bonanno DR, Frazer AK, Howatson G, Pearce AJ
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis establishing reduced intracortical inhibition as a dominant and consistent neural signature of strength training. Demonstrates measurable corticospinal adaptations following resistance training, supporting the neural contribution to early strength gains. Highly cited (157 citations) foundation for understanding training-induced neuroplasticity in rehabilitation.
key_points: Strength training consistently reduces intracortical inhibition measured via TMS
Corticospinal adaptations are measurable and significant following resistance training programmes
Reduced inhibition contributes to greater voluntary motor output and early strength gains
157 citations — foundational synthesis for training-induced neuroplasticity
Provides mechanistic rationale for rapid strength improvements in Stages 1-2 rehabilitation
Adaptations are task-specific — training method affects which corticospinal pathways adapt
Supports use of isometric and dynamic loading to drive neuromotor rehabilitation
clinical_question: How does resistance training affect corticospinal excitability and inhibition, and what are the implications for rehabilitation?
applicability: Mechanistic understanding across all rehab stages. Supports early loading as a neurological as well as structural intervention.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Mechanistic synthesis — not a loading protocol. Corticospinal adaptations begin within 2-3 weeks of consistent training. Task-specificity: isometric training best for isometric strength transfer; dynamic training for dynamic strength.

progression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework.
regression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review.

title: The Effect of Resistance Training on Motor Unit Firing Properties: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Elgueta-Cancino E, Mancilla-Engine R, Martinez-Valdes E, Falla D
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis examining resistance training effects on motor unit firing properties. Explicitly concludes that evidence quality limits definitive mechanistic claims — variability in methods and high risk of bias constrain certainty. Most directly relevant synthesis for motor-unit firing mechanisms, providing an honest appraisal of what is and is not established.
key_points: Evidence for specific motor-unit firing property changes after resistance training is limited by study quality
Methodological heterogeneity constrains definitive mechanistic conclusions
Open-access (PMC) — widely accessible for clinicians and researchers
Provides honest appraisal of the limits of current motor unit firing evidence
47 citations — growing evidence base but field is methodologically challenging
Complements broader neural adaptation literature (kb_023, kb_024) with motor-unit level evidence
Relevant for understanding neuromuscular fatigue and adaptation in high-volume training
clinical_question: Does resistance training alter motor unit firing properties, and what is the certainty of this evidence?
applicability: Background mechanistic context for all rehabilitation stages. Use to calibrate confidence in claims about motor unit adaptations during patient education.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Mechanistic synthesis — not a loading protocol. Motor unit adaptations are real but their specific firing property changes are less certain than broader corticospinal adaptations.

progression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework.
regression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review.

title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Neural Adaptations following Low-Load Blood Flow Restriction Training
authors: Centner C, Lauber B, Seynnes OR, Minshull C, Mesquita RNO, Grotkasten J, Gundermann D, Häring MF, König D
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis examining neural adaptations specifically following low-load blood flow restriction (BFR) training. Demonstrates that BFR training produces neural adaptations comparable to conventional heavy loading at lower absolute loads — directly relevant for contexts where heavy loading is contraindicated or poorly tolerated, such as high-irritability Achilles tendinopathy.
key_points: Low-load BFR training produces neural adaptations (reduced inhibition, altered excitability) comparable to conventional loading
BFR enables neural and hypertrophic adaptation at loads (20-30% 1RM) that avoid compressive tendon stress
Open-access (PMC) — widely accessible
88 citations — seminal for understanding BFR as a rehabilitation tool
Particularly relevant for high-irritability phases where heavy tendon loading is contraindicated
BFR may bridge Stages 1-2: enables progressive loading without exceeding pain thresholds
Neural adaptation mechanism: metabolic stress + occlusion triggers central adaptations similar to high-load training
clinical_question: Can low-load blood flow restriction training produce neural and hypertrophic adaptations comparable to conventional heavy resistance training?
applicability: Stage 1 to early Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation, particularly in high-irritability presentations where heavy loading cannot be tolerated. BFR provides a progressive loading option.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: BFR at 20-40% 1RM with 40-80% limb occlusion pressure. Rest 30-60s between sets. Contraindicated with active DVT, peripheral vascular disease, or open wounds. Requires trained supervision for cuff placement.

progression_criteria: Progress from BFR to conventional loading when pain allows. BFR is a bridge strategy, not a long-term substitute for progressive heavy loading.
regression_criteria: Discontinue BFR if pain increases, distal circulation compromised, or patient reports adverse symptoms.
contraindications: DVT, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension (relative), open wounds, pregnancy. Requires qualified supervision.

title: Long-Term Neurophysiological Adaptations to Strength Training: A Systematic Review With Cross-Sectional Studies
authors: Santos PDG, Vaz MA, Correia MV, Gomes TM, Correia PH, Melo BC, Feito Y, Behm D
source: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
summary: Systematic review using cross-sectional studies to examine long-term neurophysiological adaptations in resistance-trained versus untrained individuals. Demonstrates that trained individuals show greater voluntary activation, more efficient submaximal activation patterns, and distinct neurophysiological profiles. Complements intervention-based neural adaptation research with long-term training status evidence.
key_points: Long-term trained individuals show greater voluntary activation and more efficient neural patterns
Cross-sectional design captures chronic adaptation state vs acute training studies
Trained individuals demonstrate more economical submaximal activation — functional advantage for sports
Supports view that long-term training history builds neuromotor reserve relevant to injury resilience
Causal inference constrained by cross-sectional design — cannot isolate training effect from selection
Complements Stages 1-3 rehabilitation: long-term adaptation expectation-setting for patients
36 citations — newer synthesis in a growing evidence area
clinical_question: How do long-term resistance training adaptations differ neurophysiologically between trained and untrained individuals?
applicability: Return-to-sport and Stage 3 rehabilitation. Supports emphasis on long-term loading history for neuromotor resilience. Useful for patient education on the long-term value of rehabilitation.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Cross-sectional review — not a loading protocol. Long-term adaptation: neurophysiological benefits accrue over months to years of consistent training. Emphasise programme adherence and continuation post-discharge.

progression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework. Long-term adaptation supports continued training beyond formal rehabilitation.
regression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review.

title: Effects of Periodization on Strength and Muscle Hypertrophy in Volume-Equated Resistance Training Programs: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
authors: Moesgaard L, Beck MM, Christiansen L, Aagaard P, Lundbye-Jensen J
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis directly addressing periodization under the critical constraint of volume-equating. Finds periodized approaches produce modestly greater maximal strength gains than non-periodized training when volume is matched, while hypertrophy differences are less consistent. Supports periodization primarily for strength-specific neural and practice effects rather than muscle growth.
key_points: Periodized training produces modestly greater 1RM strength gains vs non-periodized when volume is equated
Hypertrophy differences between periodized and non-periodized are inconsistent — volume is the primary driver
Volume-equating is the critical methodological requirement for valid periodization comparisons
Undulating periodization may have advantages for strength in trained individuals (see kb_029)
94 citations — most relevant meta-analysis for answering the volume-equated periodization question
Informs rehabilitation programme structure: periodize for strength goals, manage volume for hypertrophy
Directly applicable to 12-week Achilles rehabilitation programme design
clinical_question: Does periodized resistance training produce superior strength and hypertrophy outcomes compared to non-periodized training when volume is equated?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation programme design. Informs whether to use periodized loading progression or simpler linear increases.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: For 12-week Achilles rehab: Phase 1 (weeks 1-4): 3x15 moderate load for familiarisation. Phase 2 (weeks 5-8): 4x10 increasing load. Phase 3 (weeks 9-12): 4x6-8 heavy load. Volume-equate between phases by adjusting load, not just reps.

progression_criteria: Advance to next phase when current rep range is completed at RPE ≤8 with pain ≤3/10 for 2 consecutive sessions.
regression_criteria: Extend current phase by 1-2 weeks if adaptation criteria not met. Reduce load rather than dropping reps if pain limits progression.
contraindications: High-irritability phase — do not begin periodized heavy loading until pain is manageable at moderate loads.

title: Effects of linear and daily undulating periodized resistance training programs on measures of muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Grgic J, Mikulic P, Podnar H, Pedisic Z
summary: Open-access systematic review and meta-analysis comparing linear periodization (LP) and daily undulating periodization (DUP) for muscle hypertrophy outcomes. Concludes that hypertrophy differences between LP and DUP are likely small, suggesting that volume is more important than periodization model for muscle mass. Trained individuals may show greater strength advantages from undulating variation.
key_points: Hypertrophy outcomes are similar between LP and DUP when volume is equated
1RM strength gains may favour DUP in trained individuals
Open-access publication (PMC) — widely accessible for clinicians
85 citations — high-quality meta-analysis for periodization model comparison
Practical implication: choose periodization model based on patient adherence and scheduling, not expected hypertrophy superiority
DUP allows more session-to-session variation — may improve adherence and motivation in rehabilitation
LP is simpler to implement and programme — appropriate for rehabilitation contexts
clinical_question: Does daily undulating periodization produce superior hypertrophy outcomes compared to linear periodization?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation programme design. LP is recommended for simplicity; DUP may offer motivational advantages for higher-level athletes.

recommended_loading_parameters.reps: variable (LP: fixed progression; DUP: varies session-to-session)
recommended_loading_parameters.notes: LP example: Week 1-4: 3x15 → Week 5-8: 4x10 → Week 9-12: 4x6-8. DUP example: Mon 3x12 / Wed 4x8 / Fri 5x5 at increasing loads. Both are valid for rehabilitation — choose based on patient profile.

progression_criteria: Same as kb_028 periodization criteria. For DUP: progress the load within each rep range, not the rep range itself.
regression_criteria: Simplify to LP if DUP variation causes confusion or adherence issues.
contraindications: High-irritability phase. Do not begin either model until moderate loading is pain-free.

title: Comparison of Powerlifting Performance in Trained Men Using Traditional and Flexible Daily Undulating Periodization
authors: Colquhoun RJ, Gai CM, Walters J, Brannon AR, Kilpatrick MW, D'Agostino DP, Campbell BI
source: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
summary: Widely cited RCT addressing flexibility and autonomy as programming features in daily undulating periodization. Compares traditional DUP (prescribed sessions) versus flexible DUP (athlete chooses daily session type within a week). Both improved strength similarly, but flexible DUP had adherence advantages. Influential for introducing autoregulation as a practical programming concept.
key_points: Flexible DUP (athlete chooses session order) produces equivalent strength gains to traditional DUP
Flexibility in programming may improve adherence without sacrificing outcomes
Pioneered practical autoregulation concept in periodization research
95 citations — widely cited in applied strength and conditioning
Implication for rehab: allowing patients some session flexibility may improve long-term adherence
Supports patient-centred approach to rehabilitation load programming
RCT in trained men — direct applicability to rehabilitation varies by population
clinical_question: Does flexibility in daily undulating periodization (patient-directed session choice) affect strength outcomes or adherence?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation — supporting patient autonomy in session scheduling within a prescribed weekly volume framework.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Flexible DUP application: prescribe 3 session types per week (e.g., heavy/moderate/light) but allow patient to choose the daily order. Maintains required weekly volume and intensity variety while supporting patient engagement.

progression_criteria: Progress overall load targets weekly regardless of session order. Review adherence at each session.
regression_criteria: Revert to prescribed session order if patient reports difficulty with self-directed scheduling.
contraindications: Patients requiring close clinical supervision should not use fully flexible programming.

title: Autoregulated resistance training for maximal strength enhancement: A systematic review and network meta-analysis
authors: Huang Z, Zhu Y, Liu M, Wang X, Yang L
summary: Contemporary systematic review and network meta-analysis capturing autoregulation strategies (APRE, RPE-based, velocity-based) for maximal strength. Indicates potential strength advantages over percentage-based loading, though the evidence base is newer and less citation-mature. Represents the current frontier of precision loading in rehabilitation and performance contexts.
key_points: Autoregulated approaches (APRE, RPE, velocity-based) may produce greater strength gains than percentage-based programming
RPE-based autoregulation is the most practically accessible method for rehabilitation contexts
Velocity-based training (VBT) requires equipment but provides real-time load feedback
Evidence is newer (2025) and less citation-mature than older periodization literature
Open-access (PMC) — accessible for clinicians
Directly applicable to Stage 2 HSR loading: RPE 8/10 target on final rep is a practical autoregulation tool
APRE (auto-regulatory progressive resistance exercise) self-adjusts load based on rep performance
clinical_question: Do autoregulated resistance training approaches produce superior strength gains compared to percentage-based loading?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation. RPE-based autoregulation (target RPE 8/10) is the recommended practical tool for session-by-session load adjustment.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: RPE autoregulation: prescribe target RPE (e.g., RPE 8 = 2 reps in reserve). Adjust load each session based on daily readiness. If RPE <8 at prescribed load, increase next set. If RPE >8, decrease. This is more responsive than fixed % programming.

progression_criteria: Progress target RPE from 7 to 8 to 9 across phases as capacity and tolerance improve.
regression_criteria: Lower target RPE (from 8 to 7) during high-pain periods or after load spikes.
contraindications: RPE autoregulation requires patient understanding of perceived exertion — provide education before implementing.

title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations
authors: Coleman M, Blazevich AJ, Androulakis-Korakakis P, Wolf M, Androulakis-Korakakis P, Schoenfeld BJ
summary: Controlled training study providing rare direct evidence on the effects of a planned deload week during resistance training. Finds that midpoint deloading may blunt strength gains without affecting hypertrophy, challenging the universal recommendation for planned deload weeks. Highly practical for fatigue management and long-term programme design.
key_points: Midpoint deload may blunt strength gains without affecting hypertrophy outcomes
Challenges the universal recommendation for planned deload weeks in all programmes
Deloading may be more beneficial when fatigue is evident than as a routine scheduled strategy
17 citations — newer but directly clinically relevant controlled evidence
Supports symptom-guided (reactive) deloading over prophylactic scheduled deloading
Relevant for Achilles rehabilitation: reduce load when next-day pain increases, not on a fixed schedule
Open-access (PeerJ)
clinical_question: Should deload weeks be routinely planned in resistance training programmes, and what is the effect on strength and hypertrophy?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation load management. Supports reactive deloading (based on pain/fatigue signals) over rigid scheduled deloads.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Deload indicator: next-day pain >3/10, VISA-A decline, or subjective fatigue score ≥7/10. Reactive deload: reduce total weekly volume by 30-40% for 1 week, maintain load intensity. Do not routinely schedule deloads — use pain and fatigue signals instead.

progression_criteria: Return to full volume after 1-week deload when next-day pain returns to baseline.
regression_criteria: Extend deload if pain does not return to baseline after 1 week. Reassess irritability classification.
contraindications: Deloading should not be used as avoidance behaviour — confirm that reduced volume is driven by objective fatigue or pain signals.

title: Biomechanical insights into Achilles tendinopathy risk and protection in runners: a large prospective study 4HAIE
authors: Jandacka D, Farana R, Uchytil J, Zahradnik D, Hamill J
summary: Rare large prospective biomechanics study directly linking measured running mechanics to incident Achilles tendinopathy in runners. Identifies specific biomechanical risk variables and protective factors. Provides the strongest available prospective evidence for biomechanics-informed screening and individualised load management in runners at risk of or recovering from Achilles tendinopathy.
key_points: Specific running biomechanical variables predict incident Achilles tendinopathy in prospective design
Protective biomechanical factors identified — inform gait retraining targets
Rare prospective design with biomechanics measurement — highest evidence for running mechanics and AT risk
Open-access (CC BY) — freely available for clinicians
Only 1 citation (2026 publication) — very recent, rapidly emerging evidence
Directly informs screening and gait assessment criteria for running rehabilitation
Supports biomechanics-informed load management in return-to-running protocols
clinical_question: What running biomechanical variables predict Achilles tendinopathy onset, and which are protective?
applicability: Return-to-running Stage 3 rehabilitation and injury prevention screening. Informs gait assessment and retraining targets for runners with Achilles tendinopathy.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Biomechanics assessment paper — not a direct loading protocol. Apply findings to gait retraining: assess and address identified risk variables (e.g., foot strike pattern, ankle stiffness, loading rate) before return to running. Retraining should be gradual and paired with progressive running volume.

progression_criteria: Return to running when Stage 2 loading capacity is established, pain ≤2/10 at fast walking, and gait risk variables have been addressed.
regression_criteria: Reduce running volume and reassess gait mechanics if AT symptoms recur during running reintroduction.
contraindications: Return to running contraindicated until Stage 2 loading (HSR 4x6-8) is well tolerated and VISA-A ≥70.

criteria.label: Pain ≤2/10 during fast walking
criteria.notes: Fast walking is the minimum functional threshold before running reintroduction.

criteria.label: VISA-A ≥70 before running reintroduction
criteria.notes: VISA-A <70 contraindicates return to running.

title: Foot and ankle biomechanics during walking in older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
authors: Pol F, Lejeune C, Leteneur S, Simoneau-Buessinger E
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis identifying consistent age-related deficits in ankle plantarflexion power and range of motion during walking in older adults. Demonstrates reduced ankle propulsion mechanics as a key biomechanical consequence of ageing — directly relevant to strengthening targets, gait intervention priorities, and fall risk management in older patients with Achilles tendinopathy.
key_points: Older adults show consistent reductions in ankle plantarflexion power and ROM during walking
Reduced ankle propulsion is a key biomechanical deficit associated with ageing
Directly informs strengthening targets: calf muscle strength and power are priority outcomes in older patients
Relevant to fall risk management and walking economy in ageing populations
36 citations — high-value synthesis for ageing-related foot/ankle mechanics
Supports age-specific modification of Stage 2 loading targets (power development as well as strength)
Older patients with Achilles tendinopathy may have compounded deficits — require staged loading approach
clinical_question: How does ageing affect ankle plantarflexion biomechanics during walking, and what are the rehabilitation implications?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation in older patients (>60 years). Informs strengthening priorities (plantarflexion power and range) and walking gait retraining targets.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: For older adults: add plantarflexion power exercises (explosive concentric phase) alongside slow eccentric loading. Include seated calf raises for isolated soleus work. Address walking economy with progressive walking challenge.

progression_criteria: Progress to single-leg standing calf raises and power-focused raises when double-leg is pain-free. Target self-selected walking speed improvement as a functional outcome.
regression_criteria: Reduce to seated calf raises or supported bilateral if pain or balance limits standing exercises.
contraindications: Balance-limiting conditions (severe peripheral neuropathy, vestibular disorders) — modify to supported exercises.

title: The influence of population characteristics and measurement system on barefoot plantar pressures: A systematic review and meta-regression analysis
authors: Telfer S, Bigham JJ
summary: Systematic review and meta-regression quantifying how plantar pressure values are systematically affected by both measurement system choice and participant characteristics (age, sex, BMI). Establishes that barefoot plantar pressure values cannot be naively compared across studies using different equipment or populations. Critical methodological reference for interpreting foot-loading data in clinical and research contexts.
key_points: Measurement system choice materially affects plantar pressure values — systems are not interchangeable
Participant characteristics (age, sex, BMI, foot size) systematically influence plantar pressure
Meta-regression approach quantifies the magnitude of these systematic biases
42 citations — methodologically seminal for plantar pressure literature
Clinical implication: serial plantar pressure measurements should use the same system for valid comparison
Warns against cross-study comparisons of foot-loading data without accounting for measurement factors
Relevant for Achilles rehabilitation monitoring: consistent measurement protocols are essential
clinical_question: How do measurement system choice and patient characteristics affect plantar pressure values, and what are the implications for clinical interpretation?
applicability: Clinical assessment and monitoring across all stages. Use the same measurement system for serial assessments. Avoid comparing plantar pressure data collected with different instruments.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Methodological reference — not a loading protocol. Standardise plantar pressure measurement protocol: same system, same conditions, same footwear status (barefoot), same time of day where possible.

progression_criteria: N/A — methodological framework.
regression_criteria: N/A — methodological framework.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review.

title: Exercise Effects on the Biomechanical Properties of the Achilles Tendon: A Systematic Review
authors: Yu C, Mei Z, Hua C, Xu Z
summary: Systematic review bridging exercise intervention and Achilles tendon biomechanical adaptation. Demonstrates that loading protocols drive measurable structural and mechanical changes in the Achilles tendon including increased stiffness, cross-sectional area, and improved energy storage and release capacity. Provides the mechanistic evidence for why loading is not only safe but structurally restorative in tendinopathy rehabilitation.
key_points: Exercise loading drives measurable Achilles tendon biomechanical adaptations: increased stiffness, CSA, and energy storage
Tendon mechanical properties improve with both eccentric and heavy slow resistance loading
Structural tendon adaptation occurs over 8-12+ weeks of consistent loading
Open-access (PMC) — widely accessible
Provides mechanistic rationale for loading-based rehabilitation: not just symptom management but structural restoration
27 citations — growing evidence base for tendon biomechanical adaptation
Directly supports Stage 2 loading rationale: drive tissue-level tendon adaptation through progressive load
clinical_question: Does exercise loading produce measurable biomechanical adaptations in the Achilles tendon, and what are the implications for rehabilitation?
