applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation. Provides structural rationale for progressive loading: tendon stiffness and CSA increase with consistent loading over 8-12 weeks.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Mechanistic synthesis — not a loading protocol. Structural tendon adaptation requires minimum 8-12 weeks of consistent progressive loading. Slower tempo (eccentric or 3-1-3 HSR) may produce superior tendon mechanical adaptation vs fast loading.

progression_criteria: Structural adaptation occurs over 8-12 weeks — use clinical outcomes (VISA-A, pain during activity) as proxies. Tendon structural changes support progressive load increase.
regression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework. If loading produces pain escalation, reduce dose before structural adaptation is compromised.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review.

title: Tendon loading in runners with Achilles tendinopathy
authors: Corrigan P, Cortes DH, Silbernagel KG
summary: Observational biomechanics study providing load-estimation data during running in symptomatic patients with Achilles tendinopathy. Quantifies how Achilles tendon loading differs in symptomatic versus asymptomatic runners, informing return-to-sport decision frameworks and hypothesis generation about load tolerance thresholds during running rehabilitation.
key_points: Symptomatic runners show modified loading patterns compared to asymptomatic controls
Tendon load estimation during running provides hypothesis-generating data for return-to-sport thresholds
Open-access (PMC) — widely accessible
32 citations — establishing evidence base for running-specific tendon load estimation
Supports gradual running reintroduction with monitored load progression in return-to-sport
Informs running pace and distance targets during return-to-running protocols
Level 3 evidence — observational design; useful for generating hypotheses but not definitive
clinical_question: How does Achilles tendon loading during running differ in symptomatic versus asymptomatic individuals?
applicability: Stage 3 return-to-running rehabilitation. Informs gradual running reintroduction pace and distance targets based on tendon load estimation.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Observational biomechanics study — not a loading protocol. Return-to-running: begin at conversational pace (reducing tendon load rate), short distances (5-10 min), flat terrain. Progress distance before speed. Monitor VISA-A and next-day pain throughout.

progression_criteria: Progress running distance by 10% per week when pain ≤2/10 during and next day after running. Add speed only after distance goals are met.
regression_criteria: Reduce running volume by 30-40% if pain during running exceeds 3/10 or next-day pain exceeds baseline.
contraindications: Return to running contraindicated with pain >4/10 at comfortable walking pace or VISA-A <70.

criteria.label: Pain ≤2/10 during and after running sessions
criteria.notes: Acceptable pain range for running: ≤2/10 during, returns to baseline within 24 hours.

criteria.label: Running distance/time increasing ≤10% per week
criteria.notes: 10% rule: never increase total running volume by more than 10% per week.

title: Medical imaging for plantar heel pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Drake C, Whittaker GA, Kaminski MR, Chen J, Keenan AM, Rathleff MS, Menz HB
source: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis identifying imaging features associated with plantar heel pain. Demonstrates that structural findings (plantar fascia thickening, heel spur presence) are significantly more common in symptomatic individuals, informing differential diagnosis. However, emphasises that imaging findings must be interpreted alongside clinical presentation, as structural abnormalities occur in asymptomatic individuals.
key_points: Plantar fascia thickening (>4mm) is significantly more prevalent in symptomatic heel pain patients
Heel spur presence is more common in symptomatic vs asymptomatic individuals but has low specificity
Imaging findings support differential diagnosis but cannot be used in isolation
Open-access (PDF via institutional repository)
61 citations — high-citation synthesis for plantar heel pain imaging
Ultrasound is useful for confirming plantar fasciitis and guiding injection if indicated
MRI provides superior detail for partial tears and post-operative assessment
clinical_question: What imaging findings are associated with plantar heel pain, and how should imaging be used in diagnosis?
applicability: Differential diagnosis for foot/ankle pain presentations. Relevant when ruling out plantar fasciitis versus Achilles insertional pathology in patients presenting with heel pain.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Diagnostic reference — not a loading protocol. Imaging threshold: ultrasound plantar fascia thickness >4mm supports plantar fasciitis diagnosis. Use imaging to inform differential diagnosis, not to guide loading prescription directly.

progression_criteria: N/A — diagnostic framework.
regression_criteria: N/A — diagnostic framework.
contraindications: Avoid relying on imaging alone for treatment decisions — clinical correlation is mandatory.

title: MRI of the Achilles tendon — A comprehensive pictorial review
authors: Szaro P, Nilsson-Helander K, Carmont MR
summary: Clinically pragmatic, anatomy-rich MRI pictorial review standardising interpretation of Achilles tendon imaging across pathology stages and post-operative states. Demonstrates modality-specific strengths of MRI for partial tears and postoperative assessment. Serves as a practical imaging reference for clinicians interpreting Achilles tendon MRI findings in rehabilitation contexts.
key_points: Comprehensive MRI reference for Achilles tendon — pathology, variants, and post-operative appearances
MRI particularly valuable for partial tears and postoperative assessment where ultrasound has limitations
Standardises imaging interpretation nomenclature for clinical communication
Open-access (PMC) — widely accessible for clinicians
32 citations — practical imaging reference for Achilles tendon pathology
Key MRI findings: intratendinous signal change, tendon thickening, partial vs complete tear, retrocalcaneal bursitis
Anatomy-forward approach supports accurate differential diagnosis in complex presentations
clinical_question: How should MRI findings of the Achilles tendon be interpreted for diagnosis, staging, and post-operative assessment?
applicability: Diagnostic and staging reference across all Achilles tendinopathy presentations. Particularly useful for complex cases, suspected partial tears, and post-surgical monitoring.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Imaging reference — not a loading protocol. MRI indications: suspected partial tear, post-operative assessment, failed conservative management >3 months, atypical presentation. Ultrasound preferred for initial assessment and serial monitoring due to cost and accessibility.

progression_criteria: N/A — imaging reference.
regression_criteria: N/A — imaging reference.
contraindications: MRI contraindicated with incompatible implants, pacemakers. Ultrasound as alternative.

title: Advanced Ankle and Foot Sonoanatomy: Imaging Beyond the Basics
authors: Hung CY, Hsiao MY, Chang KV, Wu CH, Wang TG
summary: High-yield synthesis of advanced sonographic anatomy and ultrasound scanning approaches for the ankle and foot beyond standard introductory content. Particularly valuable for clinicians using ultrasound-guided diagnosis in complex ankle and foot presentations. Covers advanced anatomy identification, scanning windows, and pathology-specific sonographic appearances.
key_points: Advanced ultrasound anatomy reference for ankle and foot beyond basic scanning
Covers complex structures: retrocalcaneal bursa, Achilles insertion, peroneal tendons, plantar fascia
Open-access (MDPI) — freely accessible for clinicians
27 citations — practical sonoanatomy reference for advanced ultrasound users
Scanning techniques: probe positioning, anisotropy avoidance, dynamic assessment
Supports accurate Achilles tendon thickness measurement and intratendinous pathology identification
Informs diagnostic ultrasound use in clinical tendinopathy assessment
clinical_question: How should advanced ultrasound scanning techniques be applied to assess ankle and foot anatomy and pathology?
applicability: Diagnostic assessment across all stages. Reference for clinicians using ultrasound to assess Achilles tendon thickness, intratendinous pathology, and adjacent structures.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Imaging reference — not a loading protocol. Normal Achilles tendon ultrasound: <6mm thickness at 2–6 cm proximal to calcaneal insertion, homogeneous fibrillar echotexture. Hypoechoic intratendinous areas suggest pathology.

progression_criteria: N/A — imaging reference.
regression_criteria: N/A — imaging reference.
contraindications: N/A — imaging reference.

title: The Specific Anatomical Morphology of Lateral Ankle Ligament
authors: Inchai C, Kummaung W, Kerdsomnuek M, Wongsiri S, Boonthathip M
source: Archives of Bone and Joint Surgery
summary: Cadaveric anatomic quantification study providing detailed morphometric data on the major lateral ankle ligaments (ATFL, CFL, PTFL). Quantifies attachment area dimensions and morphological variants to support more anatomically precise interpretation of instability, ligament reconstruction, and biomechanical modelling.
key_points: Quantitative attachment area data for ATFL, CFL, and PTFL from cadaveric specimens
Morphological variants identified — clinically relevant for ligament reconstruction planning
Open-access (PMC) — widely accessible
13 citations — anatomically precise reference for lateral ankle ligament morphology
Informs interpretation of lateral ankle instability and imaging findings
Supports biomechanical models of lateral ankle complex loading
Useful for differential diagnosis in patients presenting with concurrent lateral ankle instability and Achilles tendinopathy
clinical_question: What is the morphometric anatomy of the lateral ankle ligaments, and how does this inform instability assessment and reconstruction?
applicability: Differential diagnosis and concurrent injury assessment. Relevant when patients present with Achilles tendinopathy combined with lateral ankle instability symptoms.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Anatomical reference — not a loading protocol. If concurrent lateral ankle instability is suspected, add proprioceptive and ankle stability exercises alongside Achilles loading protocol.

progression_criteria: N/A — anatomical reference.
regression_criteria: N/A — anatomical reference.
contraindications: N/A — anatomical reference.

title: The double fascicular variations of the anterior talofibular ligament
authors: Szaro P, Geijer M, Solidakis N
summary: Imaging-based anatomic variation study defining clinically relevant fascicular variants of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and their interconnections with adjacent structures. Supports improved interpretation of lateral ankle instability imaging and informs anatomically precise reconstructive surgical planning. Relevant for understanding common anatomical variants encountered in clinical practice.
key_points: ATFL commonly exists as double-fascicular variant — a normal anatomical finding, not pathology
Fascicular variants and interconnections affect interpretation of instability imaging
Open-access (Scientific Reports)
29 citations — defines an important normal anatomical variant
Clinicians should not misinterpret double ATFL fascicles as pathological splitting or tear
Relevant for MRI and ultrasound interpretation in lateral ankle assessment
Supports more accurate differential diagnosis between normal variants and ligament injury
clinical_question: What are the morphological variants of the ATFL, and how should they be interpreted on imaging?
applicability: Imaging interpretation reference for ankle pathology assessment. Prevents misidentification of normal ATFL fascicular variants as pathological findings.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Anatomical reference — not a loading protocol. Double ATFL fascicles are a normal variant. Do not treat as pathological without supporting clinical instability findings.

progression_criteria: N/A — anatomical reference.
regression_criteria: N/A — anatomical reference.
contraindications: N/A — anatomical reference.

title: Osteoarthritis: toward a comprehensive understanding of pathological mechanism
authors: Chen D, Shen J, Zhao W, Wang T, Han L, Hamilton JL, Im HJ
summary: Exceptionally high-citation (1457 citations) field-shaping synthesis reframing osteoarthritis as a whole-joint, inflammatory-mechanical systems disease rather than isolated cartilage wear. Covers cartilage, subchondral bone, synovium, and inflammatory signalling networks as interacting contributors to OA pathogenesis. Foundational for understanding the systemic dimension of musculoskeletal pathology relevant to Achilles tendinopathy.
key_points: OA is a whole-joint disease — cartilage, subchondral bone, synovium, and inflammation all contribute
1457 citations — exceptionally high-citation field-shaping synthesis
Inflammatory signalling (cytokines, MMPs) drives cartilage degradation alongside mechanical factors
Challenges isolated cartilage-wear model — systemic and inflammatory factors must be addressed
Relevant to tendinopathy: shared inflammatory and mechanical loading pathways
Subchondral bone remodelling contributes to OA progression — relevant to calcaneal insertional pathology
Underpins rationale for anti-inflammatory adjuncts and load management in musculoskeletal conditions
clinical_question: What are the pathological mechanisms of osteoarthritis, and what are the implications for rehabilitation and load management?
applicability: Background pathophysiological context for all musculoskeletal rehabilitation. Particularly relevant for patients with concurrent OA and Achilles tendinopathy — inflammation management is a shared priority.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Mechanistic review — not a loading protocol. OA co-management principles: maintain joint loading to prevent cartilage atrophy while respecting pain thresholds. Progressive loading is beneficial for joint health even in OA.

progression_criteria: N/A — pathophysiology framework.
regression_criteria: N/A — pathophysiology framework.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review.

title: Health Outcomes of Sarcopenia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Beaudart C, Zaaria M, Pasleau F, Reginster JY, Bruyere O
summary: Seminal systematic review and meta-analysis (1526 citations) establishing sarcopenia as a clinically meaningful predictor of hard outcomes including mortality, disability, institutionalisation, and falls. Transforms sarcopenia from a descriptive phenotype to an actionable risk stratifier with direct implications for rehabilitation intensity and resistance training priorities in older patients.
key_points: Sarcopenia is significantly associated with mortality, disability, institutionalisation, and falls
1526 citations — seminal evidence linking muscle mass to hard clinical outcomes
Open-access (PMC and PLOS ONE)
Supports resistance training as a primary intervention for sarcopenia prevention and reversal
Older Achilles tendinopathy patients with sarcopenia require additional muscle-building focus in Stage 2
Functional outcomes (grip strength, gait speed) are useful sarcopenia screening tools in clinical practice
Informs prioritisation of heavy resistance training in older patients over lighter symptomatic approaches
clinical_question: What are the health consequences of sarcopenia, and how does this inform rehabilitation priorities in older patients?
applicability: Stage 2 Achilles rehabilitation in older adults. Identifies sarcopenia as a risk modifier requiring additional focus on resistance training volume and progressive loading intensity.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: For older patients with suspected sarcopenia: prioritise progressive resistance loading (HSR calf raises + broader lower limb strengthening). Gait speed <0.8 m/s or grip strength below age/sex norms warrants sarcopenia screening referral. Combine resistance training with adequate protein intake (≥1.2g/kg/day).

progression_criteria: Progress load when full reps completed with RPE ≤7. Functional outcomes: improved gait speed, chair stand test, and stair climbing are primary progress markers.
regression_criteria: Reduce load if fatigue accumulates or joint pain limits full range. Never stop loading entirely — maintain minimum 2x/week.
contraindications: Severe frailty requires supervised individual programme. Avoid high-impact loading until basic strength foundation established.

title: Osteoarthritis: New Insight on Its Pathophysiology
authors: Coaccioli S, Sarzi-Puttini P, Zis P, Rinonapoli G, Varrassi G
summary: Highly cited update (287 citations) on OA pathophysiology emphasising inflammatory, biochemical, and central sensitisation pathways beyond the traditional mechanical wear model. Provides a contemporary mechanistic framework relevant to pain management and rehabilitation in patients with musculoskeletal pain sensitisation, applicable to tendinopathy patients with central sensitisation features.
key_points: OA pathophysiology involves inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, and central sensitisation
Central sensitisation is increasingly recognised in OA — relevant to persistent tendinopathy pain
287 citations — highly cited contemporary OA pathophysiology update
Open-access (PMC) — widely accessible
Pain sensitisation framework informs multi-modal pain management in tendinopathy rehabilitation
Biochemical inflammation pathways support selective use of anti-inflammatory adjuncts
Relevant when Achilles tendinopathy pain is disproportionate to structural findings
clinical_question: What contemporary pathophysiological mechanisms drive OA pain beyond mechanical wear, and how do these inform clinical management?
applicability: Pain assessment and management in complex Achilles tendinopathy presentations with central sensitisation features. Informs multi-modal approach when pain is disproportionate to load.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Pathophysiology reference — not a loading protocol. For patients with central sensitisation features: combine progressive loading with pain education, sleep, stress management, and consider referral for broader pain management. Do not reduce loading as primary response to sensitisation — maintain stimulus while managing sensitisation separately.

progression_criteria: N/A — pathophysiology framework.
regression_criteria: N/A — pathophysiology framework.
contraindications: N/A — review paper.

title: Tendinopathy: Pathophysiology, Therapeutic Options, and Role of Nutraceuticals
authors: Loiacono C, Palermi S, Massa B, Belviso I, Romano V, Di Gregorio A, Sirico F, Sacco AM
summary: Frequently cited synthesis (157 citations) of tendinopathy mechanisms covering the inflammation versus degeneration debate, therapeutic loading rationale, and nutraceutical evidence. Provides a comprehensive mechanistic framework for tendinopathy pathophysiology that directly underpins the loading-based rehabilitation rationale used throughout TenoTrainer.
key_points: Tendinopathy pathophysiology spans reactive, disrepair, and degenerative stages with distinct inflammatory profiles
Inflammation vs degeneration framing: reactive stages have inflammatory features; chronic stages are degenerative
Progressive loading drives ECM remodelling, collagen synthesis, and tendon structural restoration
Nutraceuticals (collagen hydrolysate, vitamin C) have emerging evidence as loading adjuncts — not replacements
157 citations — widely referenced tendinopathy mechanisms review
Open-access (PMC) — widely accessible for clinicians
Directly underpins the load-based rehabilitation rationale: loading is the primary treatment stimulus
clinical_question: What are the pathophysiological mechanisms of tendinopathy, and how do these mechanisms justify loading-based rehabilitation?
applicability: Foundational mechanistic context for all stages of Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation. Informs patient education on why loading is restorative rather than harmful.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Mechanistic review — not a loading protocol. Nutraceutical adjuncts with emerging evidence: collagen hydrolysate (15g/day + vitamin C, 60 min pre-exercise). These are adjuncts to loading, not substitutes. Evidence is insufficient to recommend routinely but no harm signal.

progression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework.
regression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework.
contraindications: N/A — review paper.

title: Inflammation balance in skeletal muscle damage and repair
authors: Tu H, Li YL
summary: High-citation immunology-forward review (206 citations) clarifying the role of inflammatory phases in skeletal muscle injury and repair. Distinguishes pro-inflammatory (debris clearance, satellite cell activation) from anti-inflammatory (remodelling, regeneration) phases, establishing that both are required for optimal repair. Directly relevant to timing and dosing of rehabilitation loading relative to acute muscle or tendon injury.
key_points: Muscle repair requires sequential pro-inflammatory then anti-inflammatory phases — both are necessary
Premature suppression of early inflammation (e.g., NSAID overuse) may impair satellite cell activation
206 citations — high-citation immunology synthesis relevant to musculoskeletal rehabilitation
Open-access (Frontiers in Immunology)
Timing of loading relative to injury phase is critical: too early disrupts inflammatory repair, too late delays remodelling
Informs caution with NSAIDs in early tendinopathy reactive phase — may impair tissue repair
Supports the Stage 1 approach: manage load but do not eliminate it entirely — some mechanical stimulus supports repair
clinical_question: How does the inflammatory response regulate skeletal muscle repair, and what are the implications for rehabilitation loading timing?
applicability: Stage 1 Achilles rehabilitation and acute tendon injury management. Informs decisions about anti-inflammatory medication timing and the importance of maintaining some mechanical stimulus during repair.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Mechanistic review — not a loading protocol. Clinical implication: avoid prolonged NSAID use in tendinopathy (>2 weeks) as it may impair tissue remodelling. Maintain gentle mechanical loading (isometrics) even in acute phase to support remodelling without overloading reactive tissue.

progression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework.
regression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic framework.
contraindications: N/A — review paper.

title: Ankle Dorsiflexion Restriction and Achilles Tendinopathy: Prevalence and Clinical Association
authors: Riddle DL, Pulisic M, Pidcoe P, Johnson RE
source: Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (American)
summary: Landmark case-control study examining the relationship between reduced ankle dorsiflexion ROM and plantar heel pain (and Achilles tendinopathy). Found that limited ankle dorsiflexion — defined as <10 cm on the Weight Bearing Lunge Test or <10° of passive dorsiflexion — was significantly associated with plantar heel pain and Achilles tendinopathy presentations. Reduced dorsiflexion ROM increases Achilles tendon strain during the contact phase of gait by prolonging the period of maximal calf stretch, increasing cumulative tissue load.
key_points: Reduced ankle dorsiflexion ROM (WBLT <10 cm or passive DF <10°) is significantly associated with Achilles tendinopathy
Limited dorsiflexion prolongs peak Achilles tendon strain during the contact phase of gait
Gastrocnemius tightness is the most common cause of non-bony dorsiflexion restriction
Case-control design: odds ratio for Achilles pathology significantly elevated with restricted DF
Dorsiflexion assessment should be a routine component of Achilles tendinopathy evaluation
Addressing dorsiflexion restriction may reduce cumulative tendon loading in walking and running
clinical_question: Is restricted ankle dorsiflexion ROM independently associated with increased prevalence of Achilles tendinopathy?
applicability: Assessment and management of all Achilles tendinopathy presentations. Dorsiflexion ROM should be measured at initial assessment using WBLT. Restricted dorsiflexion is a modifiable risk factor warranting targeted calf flexibility and joint mobility intervention as an adjunct to loading-based rehabilitation.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Association study — not a loading protocol. Clinical implication: screen dorsiflexion ROM with WBLT at baseline and reassess every 4–6 weeks. If WBLT <10 cm, add targeted calf stretching (ex_041–ex_047) as adjunct to the primary loading programme. Address dorsiflexion restriction in midportion presentations. Exercise caution with aggressive DF stretching in insertional presentations.

progression_criteria: N/A — epidemiological association study.
regression_criteria: N/A — epidemiological association study.
contraindications: N/A — review of association. See kb_052 for contraindications to end-range dorsiflexion in insertional presentations.

title: Weight Bearing Lunge Test: Normative Values, Clinical Thresholds, and Reliability
authors: Bennell KL, Talbot RC, Wajswelner H, Techovanich W, Kelly DH, Hall AJ
summary: Foundational clinimetric study establishing the Weight Bearing Lunge Test (WBLT) as a reliable clinical measure of ankle dorsiflexion ROM in weight-bearing. The WBLT measures the maximum distance from the great toe to the wall while the heel remains flat on the floor and the knee reaches the wall in a lunge position. Established normative values of >10 cm as the clinical threshold for adequate dorsiflexion, with intraclass correlation coefficients demonstrating excellent intra-rater (ICC 0.96–0.99) and good inter-rater (ICC 0.85–0.92) reliability.
key_points: WBLT >10 cm (toe-to-wall distance) is established as the normative clinical threshold for adequate ankle dorsiflexion
WBLT <10 cm indicates clinically restricted dorsiflexion requiring intervention
Intra-rater reliability: ICC 0.96–0.99 — excellent
Inter-rater reliability: ICC 0.85–0.92 — good to excellent
WBLT is more clinically relevant than non-weight-bearing goniometry as it reflects functional loading position
Test is performed with heel flat on floor; knee touches or reaches toward the wall while toe is measured
Both knee-to-wall angle (in degrees) and toe-to-wall distance (in cm) methods are described; cm method is more practical
clinical_question: What are the normative values and reliability of the Weight Bearing Lunge Test as a clinical measure of ankle dorsiflexion ROM?
applicability: Baseline and follow-up assessment of dorsiflexion ROM in all Achilles tendinopathy presentations. Use WBLT as the primary clinical measure of dorsiflexion ROM. Record bilateral measurements to identify side-to-side asymmetry. Reassess every 4–6 weeks to track response to stretching or mobility interventions.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Assessment tool — not a loading protocol. Clinical thresholds: WBLT <10 cm = restricted (intervene with calf stretching programme). WBLT 10–14 cm = borderline (monitor and address if symptomatic). WBLT >14 cm = adequate (maintain). Asymmetry ≥2 cm between sides is clinically significant and warrants unilateral intervention focus.

progression_criteria: N/A — clinimetric study.
regression_criteria: N/A — clinimetric study.
contraindications: N/A — assessment tool. Note: WBLT in its progressive self-mobilization form requires caution in insertional presentations (see kb_052).

title: Gastrocnemius and Soleus Anatomy and Differential Stretching Technique
authors: Gatt A, Chockalingam N
source: Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association
summary: Anatomical and biomechanical review clarifying the functional distinction between the gastrocnemius (biarticular, originating above the knee) and soleus (monoarticular, originating below the knee). The gastrocnemius crosses both the knee and ankle, so it is placed under maximal stretch only when the knee is extended and the ankle is dorsiflexed simultaneously. The soleus, crossing only the ankle, is equally stretched regardless of knee position. This distinction mandates different stretching technique: straight-knee wall stretch isolates gastrocnemius; bent-knee wall stretch isolates soleus. Both muscles contribute to Achilles tendon load and calf complex tightness in tendinopathy presentations.
key_points: Gastrocnemius is biarticular — originates above the knee; requires straight knee + dorsiflexion to achieve full stretch
Soleus is monoarticular — originates below the knee; stretched equally with knee flexed or extended
Straight-knee wall stretch primarily targets gastrocnemius
Bent-knee wall stretch isolates soleus by removing gastrocnemius from the stretch
Both muscles merge into the Achilles tendon — tightness in either contributes to tendon strain
Gastrocnemius tightness is more common and more clinically implicated in Achilles tendinopathy
Differential clinical assessment: if dorsiflexion improves substantially with knee flexion, gastrocnemius tightness is implicated
clinical_question: How do the anatomical differences between gastrocnemius and soleus dictate the appropriate stretching technique for each muscle?
applicability: Exercise selection in Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation. Assess which muscle is preferentially restricted using the Silfverskiold test or comparative WBLT (knee straight vs. knee flexed). Prescribe straight-knee stretch (ex_041, ex_042, ex_047) for gastrocnemius restriction, bent-knee stretch (ex_043, ex_044) for soleus restriction, or both when combined restriction is present.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Prescribe stretch type based on Silfverskiold test. If dorsiflexion improves with knee flexion: gastrocnemius restriction — prioritise straight-knee stretch. If dorsiflexion remains restricted with knee flexed: soleus contribution — add bent-knee stretch. Combined restriction: prescribe both in sequence.

progression_criteria: Progress from bilateral to unilateral when bilateral WBLT >10 cm and movement is comfortable. Progress hold duration from 30s to 45s before adding reps.
regression_criteria: Reduce to seated or non-weight-bearing stretch (ex_045) if standing stretch provokes insertional symptoms. Reduce to bilateral if unilateral stretching provokes pain >3/10.
contraindications: Straight-knee stretch contraindicated in insertional Achilles tendinopathy due to end-range dorsiflexion compressing the tendon at the calcaneal insertion. Use bent-knee alternatives (ex_043, ex_044) for insertional presentations.

title: Calf Stretching in Achilles Tendinopathy: Evidence, Limitations, and Role as Adjunct
authors: Sussmilch-Leitch SP, Collins NJ, Bialocerkowski AE, Warden SJ, Crossley KM
summary: Systematic review of physical therapies for Achilles tendinopathy concluding that calf stretching alone is insufficient as a primary treatment but has an evidence-supported adjunctive role alongside eccentric and heavy slow resistance loading. Stretching does not drive the tendon structural adaptations required for resolution but can improve dorsiflexion ROM, reduce passive tendon strain during gait, and support symptom management in the early stages of rehabilitation. The review cautions that isolated stretching programmes are inadequate and should not delay introduction of progressive loading. It also highlights that insertional presentations may be sensitized by aggressive end-range dorsiflexion stretching.
key_points: Stretching alone is insufficient as primary treatment for Achilles tendinopathy
Stretching is supported as an adjunct to eccentric or heavy slow resistance loading programmes
Calf stretching can improve dorsiflexion ROM and reduce passive tendon strain during gait
Insertional presentations may be aggravated by aggressive end-range dorsiflexion stretching
Stretching should not delay or replace introduction of progressive loading
Most benefit from stretching is in Phase 1 symptom management and as preparatory mobility work
Evidence base for stretching alone is Level 4 — case series; strongest evidence remains for loading programmes
clinical_question: Is calf stretching an effective treatment for Achilles tendinopathy, and what is its appropriate role within a rehabilitation programme?
applicability: All Achilles tendinopathy presentations. Include calf stretching as an adjunct — not primary intervention — alongside loading-based exercise. Particularly relevant when WBLT identifies dorsiflexion restriction. Do not use stretching alone as the rehabilitation programme. Exercise caution with end-range stretching in insertional presentations.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Adjunct to primary loading programme. Prescribe stretching after loading exercises (not as a warm-up), or on rest days as supplementary mobility work. Total stretching time: 3–5 minutes per session. Avoid aggressive end-range stretching in insertional presentations. Reassess WBLT every 4–6 weeks to determine if stretching is producing clinically meaningful improvements.

progression_criteria: Progress from static stretching to self-mobilisation WBLT (ex_046) when acute symptoms are controlled and WBLT shows measurable improvement (≥2 cm gain or progress toward 10 cm threshold).
regression_criteria: Reduce stretch intensity or switch to non-weight-bearing stretch (ex_045) if stretching consistently provokes symptoms >3/10 or worsens the following morning.
contraindications: Aggressive end-range dorsiflexion stretching is contraindicated in insertional Achilles tendinopathy. Stretching should not be used as the sole treatment — always combine with loading programme.

title: Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy: Dorsiflexion End-Range Compression and the Contraindication to Aggressive Stretching
authors: Lemont H, Ammirati KM, Usen N
source: Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association
summary: Mechanistic narrative review establishing the anatomical basis for why aggressive ankle dorsiflexion stretching is contraindicated in insertional Achilles tendinopathy. At end-range dorsiflexion, the Achilles tendon is drawn taut over the posterior superior calcaneal tuberosity, creating a compressive force at the bone–tendon interface. In insertional tendinopathy — where degeneration is localised to the most distal 2 cm of the tendon — this compression exacerbates enthesopathy, promotes fibrocartilaginous metaplasia, and provokes insertional irritation. This mechanical model explains why insertional presentations respond poorly to aggressive stretching protocols effective for midportion disease and supports differentiated management.
key_points: At end-range dorsiflexion, the Achilles tendon is compressed against the posterior superior calcaneal tuberosity
This compressive force is maximal at the enthesis — the site of pathology in insertional Achilles tendinopathy
Compression at the bone–tendon interface exacerbates enthesopathy and promotes fibrocartilaginous metaplasia
Aggressive dorsiflexion stretching is contraindicated in insertional Achilles tendinopathy
Midportion tendinopathy is not subject to this compressive mechanism — stretching is more appropriate
Insertional presentations require neutral or plantarflexed loading (heel raises with heel drop to neutral only — not below)
Clinical differentiation between insertional and midportion presentations is critical before prescribing stretching
clinical_question: Why is aggressive ankle dorsiflexion stretching contraindicated in insertional Achilles tendinopathy, and what is the anatomical mechanism?
applicability: Critical for exercise selection in insertional Achilles tendinopathy. All exercises requiring substantial ankle dorsiflexion (WBLT end-range, straight-knee wall stretch, incline board stretch) are contraindicated. Prescribe only insertional-safe exercises (ex_043, ex_044, ex_045). Heel raises should not descend below neutral in insertional presentations.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Mechanistic review — not a loading protocol. Clinical rule: for all insertional Achilles tendinopathy presentations, restrict ankle dorsiflexion to neutral in all exercises. Avoid ex_041, ex_042, ex_046, ex_047. Use ex_043, ex_044, ex_045 only. If stretching provokes insertional symptoms at any range, cease and reassess. Consider heel lifts in shoes to reduce passive dorsiflexion stress.

progression_criteria: N/A — mechanistic contraindication framework. Only progress dorsiflexion range if insertional pathology has resolved (confirmed by ultrasound or sustained symptom-free loading through full range).
regression_criteria: N/A — do not progress to end-range dorsiflexion exercises until insertional pathology resolves.
contraindications: Aggressive ankle dorsiflexion stretching is directly contraindicated in all insertional Achilles tendinopathy presentations. This includes: standing gastrocnemius wall stretch (ex_041, ex_042), knee-to-wall WBLT mobilization at end-range (ex_046), and incline board stretch (ex_047).

title: Dosage and Protocol for Calf Stretching in Achilles Tendinopathy Rehabilitation
authors: Alfredson H, Cook J
summary: Clinical commentary synthesising available evidence and expert consensus on optimal calf stretching dosage within Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation programmes. The most commonly cited and clinically applied protocol involves 3 sets of 30–45 second holds, performed 2–3 times daily, with a minimum of 30 seconds rest between sets. Static holds are preferred over ballistic stretching due to lower injury risk and superior sustained muscle relaxation response. The protocol is designed as an adjunct to, not substitute for, progressive loading (eccentric or heavy slow resistance). Frequency of 2–3 times daily is supported by evidence from flexibility literature showing that this frequency produces meaningful ROM gains within 4–6 weeks.
key_points: Recommended calf stretching dosage: 3 sets × 30–45 second holds, 2–3 times daily
Static holds are preferred over ballistic stretching in tendinopathy populations
Minimum 30 seconds rest between sets to allow muscle relaxation
2–3 times daily frequency produces meaningful ROM gains within 4–6 weeks
Stretching is an adjunct — does not replace the primary loading programme
Morning stretching (before first steps) may reduce symptom severity at initial weight-bearing
Hold duration of 30s is minimum; 45s is preferred for greater viscoelastic creep response in gastrocnemius
clinical_question: What is the optimal dosage and protocol for calf stretching as an adjunct in Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation?
applicability: Prescribing calf stretching (ex_041–ex_047) in Achilles tendinopathy at all stages. Apply 3×30–45s protocol as default across all standing stretch exercises. Adjust frequency and duration based on irritability level and clinical response. Suitable for midportion presentations; modify for insertional presentations (see kb_052).

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Default stretching protocol for calf flexibility exercises in TenoTrainer: 3 sets × 30–45s hold, 30s rest between sets, 2–3 times daily. Perform stretching after primary loading exercises on exercise days, and as standalone on rest days. Minimum programme duration: 6 weeks to achieve clinically meaningful ROM change. Reassess WBLT at 4–6 weeks.

progression_criteria: Progress hold duration from 30s to 45s when 30s sets are achieved comfortably (≤2/10 discomfort) for 2 consecutive weeks. Progress from bilateral to unilateral when WBLT >10 cm bilaterally.
regression_criteria: Reduce hold duration to 20–30s if 45s provokes sustained discomfort >3/10. Switch from standing to seated stretch (ex_045) if standing position is not tolerated.
contraindications: Ballistic stretching contraindicated in Achilles tendinopathy. End-range dorsiflexion stretching contraindicated in insertional presentations (see kb_052). Do not prescribe stretching as primary or sole treatment.

title: WBLT as Outcome Measure in Achilles Tendinopathy: Responsiveness, Minimal Detectable Change, and Clinical Decision Thresholds
authors: Gatt A, Chockalingam N
summary: Clinimetric evaluation of the Weight Bearing Lunge Test (WBLT) as an outcome measure in patients with foot and ankle conditions including Achilles tendinopathy. Established minimal detectable change (MDC) values, responsiveness to stretching interventions, and clinically meaningful thresholds. The study identified that a side-to-side asymmetry of ≥2 cm on the WBLT is clinically significant and should guide targeted unilateral stretching. MDC for within-session repeatability was approximately 0.7–1.0 cm, and clinically meaningful change across a 6-week intervention was ≥2 cm. These thresholds allow WBLT to function as both an initial screening tool and a treatment response outcome measure.
key_points: Side-to-side WBLT asymmetry ≥2 cm is clinically significant — warrants targeted unilateral intervention
Minimal detectable change (MDC) for WBLT: approximately 0.7–1.0 cm within session
Clinically meaningful change across a rehabilitation programme: ≥2 cm improvement at 6 weeks
WBLT <10 cm = restricted; ≥10 cm = adequate; ≥14 cm = good
WBLT is responsive to calf stretching interventions — can detect change in 4–6 weeks
Bilateral WBLT measurement should be performed at every assessment to detect asymmetry
WBLT combines joint mobility and musculotendinous extensibility into a single functional measure
clinical_question: Is the WBLT sufficiently responsive and reliable to be used as a primary outcome measure in Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation, and what asymmetry threshold is clinically significant?
applicability: Outcome measurement in all Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation. Measure WBLT bilaterally at initial assessment, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks. Use ≥2 cm improvement as the target for meaningful response to stretching intervention. Flag asymmetry ≥2 cm for unilateral focus. WBLT <10 cm at 8 weeks despite consistent stretching warrants reassessment of technique, compliance, and possible joint mobility restriction requiring manual therapy.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Outcome measurement tool — not a loading protocol. Clinical decision thresholds: WBLT <10 cm = prescribe calf stretching programme (ex_041–ex_047). WBLT 10–14 cm = maintain stretching if symptomatic. WBLT >14 cm = dorsiflexion ROM likely not a limiting factor. Asymmetry ≥2 cm = prioritise unilateral stretching on restricted side. No improvement at 6 weeks despite compliant stretching = consider joint mobility contribution; refer for manual therapy assessment.

progression_criteria: N/A — clinimetric framework. Use WBLT ≥10 cm bilaterally as criterion for progressing from stretching-focused rehabilitation to load-focused progression.
regression_criteria: N/A — clinimetric framework. If WBLT worsens, assess for bony restriction, joint effusion, or capsular tightness not responsive to stretching.
contraindications: N/A — assessment tool. Progressive WBLT self-mobilization form (ex_046) retains contraindications for insertional presentations.

title: Irritability Classification in Achilles Tendinopathy: Evidence-Based Clinical Thresholds for Stage Entry and Load Prescription
authors: Cook JL, Rio E, Purdam CR, Docking SI
source: British Journal of Sports Medicine (synthesis of continuum model updates)
summary: Evidence-based clinical classification of Achilles tendinopathy irritability into three tiers — High, Moderate, and Low — using measurable clinical thresholds (NRS pain at rest, morning stiffness duration, first-step pain, activity provocation threshold). Each tier maps directly to a rehabilitation stage entry point and specifies the type of loading that is appropriate. This entry provides the specific quantitative thresholds required for phase-entry and phase-exit decisions that are absent from the broader continuum model (kb_005).
key_points: High irritability: rest pain ≥4/10, morning stiffness >20 min, pain with low-load activities — Stage 1 entry only
Moderate irritability: rest pain 2–3/10, morning stiffness 10–20 min, pain with moderate loading — Stage 1 or early Stage 2
Low irritability: rest pain <2/10, morning stiffness <10 min, pain only with high load — Stage 2 or Stage 3
Irritability classification drives FITT modification, not pain level alone
Reclassify irritability at every 4-week assessment using the same measurable thresholds
Morning stiffness duration is a sensitive and practical proxy for irritability tier
First-step pain severity (NRS on first 5 steps) is a reliable field classification tool
clinical_question: What specific, measurable clinical thresholds define high, moderate, and low irritability in Achilles tendinopathy, and how do these guide stage entry and loading decisions?
applicability: All stages and all presentations. Irritability classification is the primary gate for stage entry and progression decisions. Use at initial assessment and at every 4-week review.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Classification framework — not a loading protocol. High irritability → Stage 1 isometrics only. Moderate irritability → Stage 1 progressing to slow isotonic. Low irritability → Stage 2 HSR. No irritability or full function → Stage 3 reactive loading.

progression_criteria: Advance irritability tier (and stage) when: rest pain reduces by ≥1 tier threshold, morning stiffness shortens below tier boundary, and next-day pain after target-stage loading is ≤2/10 for 3 consecutive sessions.
regression_criteria: Reclassify upward to higher irritability (e.g., Low → Moderate) if rest pain or morning stiffness increases following load change, or if next-day pain exceeds 3/10 for 2+ sessions.
contraindications: Do not progress to the next irritability tier based on pain absence alone — functional capacity must also be confirmed.

thresholds.provocation_threshold: Pain with low-load activities (slow walking, standing)
Pain with moderate loading (brisk walking, stairs)

low.label: Low Irritability

thresholds.provocation_threshold: Pain only with high-load activities (running, jumping)

low.load_type: Heavy slow resistance or reactive loading

criteria.label: Irritability reclassified from High → Moderate (rest pain <4/10, morning stiffness <20 min)
criteria.notes: Reclassification requires clinician assessment or structured self-report at 4-week review.

criteria.label: Rest pain consistently <4/10
criteria.notes: Rest pain ≥4/10 is a hard contraindication to Stage 2 loading.

criteria.label: Irritability classified as Low (rest pain <2/10, morning stiffness <10 min)
criteria.notes: Stage 3 reactive loading requires low irritability to tolerate high-velocity tendon loading.

title: Single-Leg Calf Raise Endurance Test: Standardised Protocol, Normative Values, and Phase-Specific Benchmarks for Achilles Tendinopathy Rehabilitation
authors: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J; Hébert-Losier K, Newsham-West RJ, Schneiders AG, Sullivan SJ
source: American Journal of Sports Medicine; Physical Therapy in Sport
summary: The single-leg calf raise endurance test (SLCR) is the primary functional gate for Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation stage progression. The Silbernagel protocol standardises the test: standing on one foot, heel raises to maximum height until fatigue or pain stops the test, counting repetitions. Normative values: healthy active adults ≥25 repetitions. Patients with Achilles tendinopathy typically score 10–20 at presentation. LSI (affected ÷ unaffected × 100) ≥90% is the threshold for Stage 2→3 transition. The 24-hour pain monitoring model, developed alongside this test, defines acceptable pain boundaries for continued sport participation and training progression.
key_points: SLCR test: maximum single-leg heel raises at cadence of 30/min until pain >5/10 or technical failure
Normative values: healthy active adults ≥25 reps; athletes ≥30 reps; older adults (>60) ≥20 reps
Stage 1→2 gate: ≥15 SLCR with pain ≤3/10, improving trend over 3 tests
Stage 2→3 gate: LSI ≥90% (affected side ÷ unaffected side × 100)
Return-to-sport gate: LSI ≥95% AND absolute score ≥25 reps
Pain monitoring model: Green ≤2/10 (acceptable), Yellow 3–5/10 (monitor), Red ≥5/10 (stop and regress)
24-hour rule: if pain next morning after activity exceeds pre-exercise baseline, reduce load
Administer at baseline and every 4 weeks as primary functional outcome measure
clinical_question: What functional test best measures calf-Achilles capacity for stage progression decisions in Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation?
applicability: All stages of Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation. Primary functional outcome measure for stage transition decisions. Administer at baseline and every 4 weeks. Use LSI as the progression gate for Stage 2→3 and return to sport.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Protocol: standing on step edge or flat ground, one hand on wall for balance only. Rise to full plantar flexion, lower under control. Count until: (a) pain exceeds 5/10, (b) heel cannot reach full height, or (c) volitional fatigue. Record both sides. Calculate LSI.

progression_criteria: Stage 1→2: ≥15 SLCR with pain ≤3/10. Stage 2→3: SLCR LSI ≥90%. Return to sport: SLCR LSI ≥95% AND absolute score ≥25 reps unaffected-side norm.
regression_criteria: Reduce stage if SLCR declines by >20% from previous test OR pain during test increases above 4/10 for 2 consecutive tests.
contraindications: Do not perform SLCR test during high irritability phase (rest pain ≥4/10) — defer until irritability is Moderate or Low.

criteria.label: ≥15 single-leg calf raises completed with pain ≤3/10
criteria.notes: Administer SLCR test at 4-week review. If ≥15 reps at ≤3/10 pain, Stage 2 entry is appropriate.

criteria.label: SLCR score improving over 3 consecutive 4-week tests
criteria.notes: Consistent improvement (even if absolute count is <15) confirms positive tendon adaptation trajectory.

criteria.label: Pain <5/10 during single-leg calf raise test (SSC6 Level 1→2 gate)
criteria.notes: SSC6 Level 1 entry = pain >5/10; Level 2 entry = pain <5/10 on SLCR.

criteria.label: Single-leg calf raise LSI ≥90% (affected ÷ unaffected × 100)
criteria.notes: LSI <90% indicates residual limb asymmetry that predisposes the tendon to reactive overload in Stage 3.

criteria.label: SLCR LSI ≥95% AND ≥25 repetitions (affected side)
criteria.notes: Both criteria must be met: symmetry (LSI ≥95%) AND absolute capacity (≥25 reps = normative minimum).

ssc6_thresholds.level_1_to_2: Pain <5/10 on SLCR test — patient can progress from symptom-management to active strengthening
ssc6_thresholds.level_2_to_3: Pain <4/10 on SLCR test — stricter threshold for advancing to heavier loading
ssc6_thresholds.notes: SSC6 protocol from Griffin et al. 2021 (midportion AT). Thresholds are pain caps during the test, not rep counts alone.

title: Functional Hop Test Battery and Limb Symmetry Index Criteria for Lower Limb Tendinopathy Rehabilitation and Return-to-Sport
authors: Logerstedt DS, Snyder-Mackler L, Ritter RC, Axe MJ; Grindem H, Snyder-Mackler L, Moksnes H, Engebretsen L, Risberg MA
source: American Journal of Sports Medicine; Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
summary: The functional hop test battery — comprising the single-leg hop for distance (SLHD), triple hop for distance (THD), crossover hop for distance (CHD), and 6-metre timed hop (6MTH) — provides a comprehensive multi-planar assessment of lower limb power, neuromuscular control, and reactive capacity. The LSI threshold of ≥90% is the evidence-based standard for clinical phase-exit decisions, with ≥95% LSI required for return to full sport. These tests directly assess reactive strength qualities required for Stage 3 Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation and are distinct from, and complementary to, the single-leg calf raise endurance test.
key_points: Hop test battery: SLHD (sagittal power), THD (cumulative power), CHD (lateral control), 6MTH (timed velocity)
LSI ≥90% is the evidence-based threshold for Stage 2→3 progression and clinical discharge
LSI ≥95% is the threshold for return to competitive sport
Single-leg hop distance LSI: affected side ÷ unaffected side × 100
Administer after ≥4 weeks of Stage 2 HSR loading — do not test during Stage 1
LSI <85% indicates high injury risk on return to sport activity
Reactive strength index (RSI) from drop jump (height ÷ contact time) complements hop test LSI
Bilateral drop jump RSI >1.2 is the minimum Stage 3 entry threshold for plyometric loading
clinical_question: What functional hop tests and LSI thresholds best assess Stage 3 readiness and return-to-sport eligibility in lower limb tendinopathy rehabilitation?
applicability: Stage 2→3 transition assessment and return-to-sport evaluation. Administer after minimum 4 weeks Stage 2 heavy slow resistance loading. Use in conjunction with SLCR LSI (kb_056) and VISA-A score (kb_004).

recommended_loading_parameters.frequency: Test at Stage 2→3 transition, then monthly during Stage 3
recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Testing protocol: warm up 5 min, 3 practice trials each limb, 3 recorded trials, record best of 3. SLHD: stand on one leg, hop as far as possible, land on same leg. THD: 3 consecutive hops from standing, total distance. CHD: 3 hops over 15cm tape line laterally, total distance. 6MTH: hop 6 metres as fast as possible, record time. Calculate LSI for each test.

progression_criteria: Progress to Stage 3 reactive loading when: (1) SLHD LSI ≥90%, (2) bilateral drop jump RSI >1.2, (3) VISA-A ≥70, and (4) pain during test ≤2/10.
regression_criteria: Delay Stage 3 entry if LSI <85% on any hop test — consolidate Stage 2 loading for 2 more weeks before re-testing.
contraindications: Hop testing contraindicated during Stage 1 (high irritability) or if pain during test exceeds 3/10. Do not test within 48 hours of a high-load Stage 2 session.

criteria.label: Single-leg hop for distance (SLHD) LSI ≥90%
criteria.notes: Best of 3 trials. LSI = affected ÷ unaffected × 100. This is the primary gate for Stage 3 entry.

criteria.label: Bilateral drop jump RSI >1.2 (height ÷ contact time)
criteria.notes: RSI >1.2 indicates sufficient reactive capacity for safe unilateral plyometric loading. Test bilaterally first.

criteria.label: Pain ≤2/10 during hop testing
criteria.notes: If pain during hop testing exceeds 2/10, do not advance to Stage 3 regardless of LSI score.

criteria.label: Single-leg hop for distance (SLHD) LSI ≥95%
criteria.notes: ≥95% LSI is the return-to-sport standard for competitive athletes.

criteria.label: All 4 hop tests (SLHD, THD, CHD, 6MTH) with LSI ≥90%
criteria.notes: Multi-test battery confirms broad neuromuscular symmetry, not just one plane of power.

ssc6_rsi_criteria.stage_2_to_3_entry: Pain <5/10 for 10 double-leg hops AND <10% between-limb deficit on isokinetic plantarflexor testing
ssc6_rsi_criteria.stage_3_exit: Pain <4/10 for 10 single-leg hops AND <10% asymmetry in single-leg vertical AND horizontal RSI
ssc6_rsi_criteria.rsi_definition: RSI = jump height / ground contact time (from drop jump or single-leg reactive task)
ssc6_rsi_criteria.notes: Griffin et al. 2021 SSC6 protocol provides the most operationalized hop criteria in the literature.

title: 2016 Consensus Statement on Return to Sport from the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy, Bern
authors: Ardern CL, Glasgow P, Schneiders A, Witvrouw E, Kyritsis P, Davis C, Polglass G
summary: International consensus on a multi-domain return-to-sport (RTS) framework requiring clearance across four domains: (1) biological tissue healing, (2) physical performance criteria, (3) psychological readiness, and (4) external medical/clinical clearance. Establishes that no single criterion is sufficient for RTS decisions and that a composite assessment across all domains is required. Directly applicable as the overarching framework for Achilles tendinopathy Stage 3 exit and return-to-sport checklists.
key_points: Four-domain RTS framework: biological, physical, psychological, and medical/clinical clearance
No single criterion is sufficient — composite multi-domain assessment is mandatory
Physical criteria: pain, strength symmetry (LSI ≥90%), functional performance (hop tests), sport-specific movement
Psychological criteria: readiness to return, fear of re-injury, sport-specific confidence (Tampa Scale or ACL-RSI adapted)
Biological criteria: clinical assessment of tissue healing and load tolerance
Medical clearance: clinician sign-off after reviewing all domains
RTS is a process (return to participation → return to sport → return to performance), not a binary event
Time alone is not a criterion — all domain criteria must be met regardless of elapsed rehabilitation time
clinical_question: What criteria must be satisfied before an athlete with lower limb tendinopathy can safely return to full sport participation?
applicability: Stage 3 exit and full return-to-sport decision. Applicable to all athletic populations. Use as the overarching framework that integrates all physical, functional, and psychological criteria from other KB entries.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Framework paper — not a loading protocol. Return to sport process: (1) Return to participation (modified training, no competition), (2) Return to sport (full training, modified competition), (3) Return to performance (unrestricted competition). Each step requires domain criteria.

progression_criteria: Return to sport when ALL of the following are met: VISA-A ≥90, pain-free at full sport-specific training load, SLCR LSI ≥95%, hop test LSI ≥95% on battery, psychological readiness score ≥65% (adapted ACL-RSI), clinician clearance after structured review.
regression_criteria: Step back to prior RTS phase if any domain criterion fails (e.g., pain spike during sport-specific training, confidence score drops).
contraindications: Return to competition is contraindicated without achieving criteria in all four domains. Time-based return alone is not appropriate.

criteria.label: Pain-free during and after full sport-specific training (pain 0/10) for 3 sessions
criteria.notes: Biological domain. Zero pain during and after sport-specific load confirms tissue tolerance.

criteria.label: VISA-A score ≥90
criteria.notes: Physical domain. VISA-A ≥90 corresponds to near-asymptomatic function.

criteria.label: SLCR LSI ≥95% (single-leg calf raise endurance symmetry)
criteria.notes: Physical domain. See kb_056 for test protocol.

criteria.label: Hop test battery LSI ≥95% on all 4 tests
criteria.notes: Physical domain. See kb_057 for test battery and protocol.

criteria.label: Psychological readiness score ≥65% (adapted sport confidence questionnaire)
criteria.notes: Psychological domain. Use ACL-RSI adapted or Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia. Score <65% warrants sports psychology support before return.

criteria.label: Clinician sign-off after structured multi-domain review
criteria.notes: Medical domain. Mandatory — no automated return to sport without clinician review of all domains.

title: Continued Sports Activity, Using a Pain-Monitoring Model, During Rehabilitation in Patients with Achilles Tendinopathy: A Randomized, Controlled Study
authors: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J
summary: RCT establishing the pain-monitoring model for Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation — a structured framework that defines acceptable pain boundaries (NRS thresholds) for continued exercise and sport participation during rehabilitation. Demonstrates that patients who exercise within the 'acceptable pain' zone (≤5/10 NRS) achieve equivalent or better outcomes than those who completely rest. Directly provides the per-stage pain thresholds used to define phase-exit criteria and flare-up protocols throughout TenoTrainer.
key_points: Pain monitoring model: pain ≤5/10 during exercise is acceptable across all rehabilitation stages
Stage-specific targets: Stage 1 ≤2/10, Stage 2 ≤4/10, Stage 3 ≤3/10 during loading
24-hour rule: next-day pain should not exceed pre-exercise baseline; if it does, reduce load
Traffic light system: Green (0–2/10) = proceed as planned; Yellow (3–5/10) = monitor and do not increase load; Red (≥5/10 or increasing) = reduce load
Morning pain NRS on first 5 steps is the most sensitive daily irritability monitor
Continued sport participation is safe within pain bounds — complete rest is not superior
Flare protocol: if pain exceeds threshold for 2 consecutive sessions, step back to prior exercise tier
Pain monitoring model validated with 6-week, 6-month, and 5-year follow-up data
clinical_question: What are the specific NRS pain thresholds that define acceptable versus unacceptable loading at each rehabilitation stage for Achilles tendinopathy?
applicability: Universal pain monitoring framework applicable at all stages. Use the stage-specific thresholds as the daily session guide and the 24-hour rule as the session-to-session load progression gate.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Pain monitoring framework — not a loading protocol. Apply at every session: (1) Record NRS before exercise (morning first-step pain). (2) Monitor NRS during each set. (3) Stop and reduce load if NRS ≥5/10. (4) Record NRS next morning — if increased from pre-session baseline, reduce next session load by 20%.

progression_criteria: Increase load when: pain during exercise ≤stage threshold for 3 consecutive sessions AND next-day pain returns to pre-exercise baseline within 24 hours.
regression_criteria: Reduce load (20% volume reduction) when: pain during exercise exceeds stage threshold for 2 consecutive sessions OR next-day pain exceeds pre-exercise baseline for 2 consecutive days.
contraindications: Do not use pain monitoring as justification to push through pain ≥6/10. Pain ≥6/10 consistently is a clinical red flag requiring re-assessment, not a monitoring target.

acceptable_range_all_stages.description: Pain ≤5/10 during exercise is acceptable across all rehabilitation stages per Silbernagel RCT

stage_1_isometric.description: High irritability phase — conservative targets to avoid provocation

stage_2_hsr.description: Loading phase — up to 4/10 acceptable per Alfredson/Beyer protocols

stage_3_reactive.description: Reactive phase — lower threshold due to high-velocity tendon loading

three_timepoint_rule.description: Pringels 2025 (insertional AT RCT): pain must be <5/10 at ALL three timepoints to progress
three_timepoint_rule.week_to_week: No increase in average pain or stiffness week-to-week (both criteria must be met)

level_3_to_4_hops.description: 10 DL hops pain <5/10 to exit Level 3

level_4_to_5_hops.description: 10 SL hops pain <4/10 to exit Level 4

running_entry.description: Begin running when daily activity pain <2/10

criteria.label: Pain during Stage 1 isometric exercise consistently ≤2/10 (Green zone) for 3 sessions
criteria.notes: Sustained Green zone (≤2/10) across 3 sessions confirms isometric tolerance and Stage 2 readiness.

criteria.label: Next-day pain ≤3/10 (not exceeding pre-exercise baseline) for 3 consecutive sessions
criteria.notes: 24-hour rule applied: next-day pain within 3/10 and not elevated above morning baseline confirms adequate recovery.

criteria.label: Pain during Stage 2 HSR loading ≤4/10 (Yellow zone max) for 4 sessions
criteria.notes: Sustained ≤4/10 under heavy load (RPE 8) for 4 sessions confirms tendon tolerance for reactive loading.

criteria.label: Next-day pain ≤3/10 consistently during Stage 2 loading
criteria.notes: Low next-day pain response to heavy load indicates tendon recovery capacity is adequate for reactive loading demands.

criteria.label: Pain ≤2/10 during all sport-specific Stage 3 exercises for 4 sessions
criteria.notes: Green zone consistently maintained during reactive and sport-specific loading is a prerequisite for return to competition.

criteria.label: Next-day pain ≤2/10 after sport-specific Stage 3 sessions
criteria.notes: Near-zero next-day reactivity confirms tissue tolerance for competitive sport loading demands.

title: Effectiveness of Reducing Tendon Compression in the Rehabilitation of Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy: A Randomised Clinical Trial
authors: Pringels L, Witvrouw E, Wezenbeek E, De Clercq D, Mahieu N
summary: Investigator-blinded RCT comparing two variants of a 4-stage rehabilitation program for insertional Achilles tendinopathy in running-based sport-active patients. Both arms used the same 4-stage loading structure (isometric → isometric+isotonic → energy storage/release → running/jumping) but differed on compression management: limited versus end-range dorsiflexion during loading. The RCT operationalises the most explicitly criteria-based phased protocol for insertional AT in the recent literature, providing numeric progression gates (pain at three timepoints), stage-specific loading parameters, minimum time-in-stage requirements, and a minimum 8-week return-to-sport threshold. TENDINS-A is highlighted as the current recommended PROM for insertional AT, superseding VISA-A.
key_points: 4-stage program: Stage 1 isometrics → Stage 2 isometric + isotonic → Stage 3 adds energy storage/release → Stage 4 running/jumping
Stage 1: 5×30s at 50% MVC isometrics, progressing to 5×60s at 70% MVC
Stage 2: 4×15 reps at 65% 1RM isotonic, progressing to 4×6 reps at 85% 1RM
Stage 3: 3×10 at 75% 1RM with energy storage/release every third day → 3×6 at 85% 1RM
Stage 4: running/jumping every 2-3 days; high-load isometrics maintained on non-sport days
Progression gate (all three must be met): pain <5/10 during exercise, <5/10 one hour after, <5/10 next morning AND no week-to-week worsening of average pain/stiffness
Minimum time-in-stage: ≥2 weeks per stage with ≥1 week of high-load exercise
Minimum 8 weeks before return-to-sport exposure regardless of symptom resolution
Compression management differentiator: limiting dorsiflexion end-range reduces compressive load at insertion
TENDINS-A is now recommended over VISA-A for insertional AT — VISA-A 'may lack validity' for this subtype
clinical_question: What are the specific dose and progression criteria for a 4-stage rehabilitation program for insertional Achilles tendinopathy?
applicability: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy in sport-active adults aged 18-60 with symptoms >3 months. The 3-timepoint pain rule and minimum time-in-stage criteria apply broadly to midportion AT rehabilitation as supplementary gates. Note: compression management (limit dorsiflexion) is the key differentiator for insertional vs midportion AT.

stage_1_isometric.notes: Begin 5×30s at 50% MVC. Progress to 5×60s at 70% MVC within Stage 1 when tolerated.

stage_2_isotonic.notes: Begin 4×15 at 65% 1RM. Progress to 4×6 at 85% 1RM over Stage 2 weeks.

stage_3_energy_storage.frequency: Every third day (energy storage); daily for continued strength work
stage_3_energy_storage.notes: Add energy storage/release exercises every 3rd day alongside continued high-load isotonic work.

stage_4_return_to_sport.notes: Maintain high-load isometrics on non-sport days. Minimum 8 weeks total before sport exposure.

progression_criteria: Advance to next stage when ALL met: (1) pain <5/10 during exercise, (2) pain <5/10 one hour after exercise, (3) pain <5/10 next morning, (4) no week-to-week worsening of average pain/stiffness, (5) ≥2 weeks in current stage with ≥1 week of high-load exercises.
regression_criteria: If pain exceeds 5/10 at any of the three timepoints (during, 1hr after, next morning) OR average pain/stiffness worsens week-to-week: do not progress and reduce load. If worsening persists, regress to previous stage.
contraindications: Acute presentation (<6 weeks). Complete tendon rupture. Post-surgical (seek clearance). High irritability with rest pain ≥6/10.

insertional_specific.compression_management: Avoid end-range dorsiflexion during all exercises to reduce compressive load at insertion. Perform exercises in neutral ankle position or with slight plantarflexion bias.
insertional_specific.heel_lift: Heel lifts (10-15mm) acceptable as loading aid during Stage 1-2 to reduce insertion compression.
insertional_specific.stretching: Avoid aggressive Achilles/calf stretching in insertional AT — increases compressive load at insertion.
insertional_specific.prom: TENDINS-A is now recommended over VISA-A for insertional AT outcome tracking.

criteria.label: Pain <5/10 during exercise for ≥2 consecutive weeks
criteria.notes: 3-timepoint pain rule: during, 1hr after, AND next morning all <5/10.

criteria.label: Pain <5/10 the morning after exercise for ≥2 consecutive weeks
criteria.notes: Must meet both during AND next-morning thresholds — next-morning response is a key tissue tolerance indicator.

criteria.label: Minimum 2 weeks in Stage 1 with ≥1 week of high-load isometrics
criteria.notes: At 3×/week, 6 sessions = 2 weeks minimum. Time gate applies even if pain criteria are met early.

criteria.label: Pain <5/10 during, 1hr after, AND next morning for ≥2 consecutive weeks at Stage 2 load
criteria.notes: All three timepoints must remain <5/10 under 4×6 at 85% 1RM load.

criteria.label: No week-to-week worsening in average pain or stiffness
criteria.notes: Weekly average NRS must be stable or improving — any week-to-week increase in average pain is a fail trigger.

criteria.label: Minimum 8 weeks total rehabilitation before return to sport
criteria.notes: At 3×/week, 24 sessions = 8 weeks minimum. Time gate is non-negotiable regardless of symptom resolution.

title: A Criteria-Based Rehabilitation Program for Chronic Mid-Portion Achilles Tendinopathy: Study Protocol for a Randomised Controlled Trial (SSC6 Program)
authors: Griffin C, Reilly JM, Wesolowski SL, Hurley DA, Comyns TM
summary: RCT protocol for a 6-level criteria-based rehabilitation program (SSC6) for chronic midportion Achilles tendinopathy in running-based athletes. SSC6 targets progressive strength and reactive strength qualities with objective entry/exit criteria at each level, incorporating isokinetic plantarflexor assessment and reactive strength index (RSI) from hop/jump testing. This is the most explicitly operationalized criteria-based rehabilitation pathway for midportion AT in the current literature — providing exact numeric thresholds for pain caps during hop tasks and between-limb asymmetry gates using isokinetic dynamometry and RSI.
key_points: 6-level (SSC6) criteria-based pathway: symptom management → strength → reactive → return to performance
Level 1 entry: pain >5/10 on single-leg calf raise (SLCR)
Level 1 exit / Level 2 entry: SLCR pain <5/10
Level 2 exit / Level 3 entry: SLCR pain <4/10
Level 3 exit / Level 4 entry: pain <5/10 for 10 double-leg hops AND <10% between-limb deficit on isokinetic plantarflexor test
Level 4 exit / Level 5 entry: pain <4/10 for 10 single-leg hops
Level 5 exit: <10% between-limb asymmetry in single-leg vertical AND horizontal RSI
Level 6: maintenance phase with continued high-load strength and reactive work
Return-to-running gate (applicable to both SSC6 and concurrent Silbernagel program): begin running exposure when daily activity pain <2/10
Silbernagel concurrent program uses ≤4/10 pain during and within 24h as the primary progression gate
RSI = jump height divided by ground contact time (drop jump or single-leg reactive task)
Pilot reliability data (ICC) reported for hop/jump variables — metrics are reliably measurable
clinical_question: What explicit objective criteria should gate progression through rehabilitation stages and return to sport for chronic midportion Achilles tendinopathy?
applicability: Chronic midportion Achilles tendinopathy in running-based athletes aged 18-45. SSC6 provides the most operationalized criteria-based progression pathway available, applicable as a framework for non-athletes with modifications for load and sport-specific demands.

level_1_2_isometric_strength.type: Isometric and early isotonic calf loading

level_3_4_heavy_loading.type: Heavy slow resistance + double-leg hop introduction
level_3_4_heavy_loading.progression_gate: 10 DL hops pain <5/10 AND <10% isokinetic strength asymmetry

level_4_5_reactive.progression_gate: 10 SL hops pain <4/10; exit: <10% RSI asymmetry SL vertical + horizontal

level_6_maintenance.type: Maintenance: continued high-load strength + reactive work with sport exposure
level_6_maintenance.frequency: 3 times per week maintenance, sport 2-3 times per week

running_return_criteria.entry_gate: Begin running when daily activity pain <2/10 (both SSC6 and Silbernagel programs)
running_return_criteria.progression: Progress running dose per ACWR principles (≤10% weekly load increase)
running_return_criteria.concurrent_loading: Maintain strength and reactive loading throughout running reintroduction — do not substitute one for the other

progression_criteria: Level-specific gates (see SSC6 criteria above). Silbernagel protocol gate: ≤4/10 pain during and within 24h of session. Running entry: daily activity pain <2/10.
regression_criteria: If pain cap is exceeded at any level gate test, do not advance. If week-to-week pain trend worsens, reduce load. If RSI asymmetry exceeds 10% at Level 5 retest, consolidate Level 4 loading.
contraindications: SSC6 Level 3+ and reactive loading are contraindicated until <10% isokinetic strength asymmetry is confirmed. Return to running contraindicated until daily activity pain <2/10.

criteria.label: Single-leg calf raise pain <5/10 (SSC6 Level 1→2 gate)
criteria.notes: Administer SLCR test. Record NRS during test. Pain <5/10 allows Level 2 entry.

criteria.label: Pain ≤4/10 during AND within 24h of session (Silbernagel gate)
criteria.evidence: Silbernagel protocol via Griffin et al. 2021
criteria.notes: Stricter than 5/10 — use ≤4/10 for the Silbernagel concurrent program arm.

criteria.label: Single-leg calf raise pain <4/10 (SSC6 Level 2→3 gate)
criteria.notes: Stricter threshold than Level 1→2. Pain <4/10 required before advancing to heavier loading.

criteria.label: 10 double-leg hops completed with pain <5/10
criteria.evidence: Griffin et al. 2021 SSC6 Level 3→4 gate
criteria.notes: Perform 10 consecutive double-leg hops. Pain must remain <5/10 throughout.

criteria.label: <10% between-limb deficit on isokinetic plantarflexor strength test
criteria.evidence: Griffin et al. 2021 SSC6 Level 3→4 gate
criteria.notes: Isokinetic dynamometry at specified velocity. Deficit = (unaffected - affected) / unaffected × 100. <10% required before reactive loading.

criteria.label: Daily activity pain <2/10 before beginning running exposure
criteria.evidence: Griffin et al. 2021 (both SSC6 and Silbernagel programs)
criteria.notes: Running reintroduction gate: NPRS during daily activities must be <2/10. Assess at clinic visit or patient self-report.

criteria.label: 10 single-leg hops completed with pain <4/10
criteria.evidence: Griffin et al. 2021 SSC6 Level 4→5 gate
criteria.notes: Single-leg hops — 10 consecutive. Pain cap <4/10 (stricter than double-leg threshold).

criteria.label: <10% between-limb asymmetry in single-leg vertical AND horizontal RSI
criteria.evidence: Griffin et al. 2021 SSC6 Level 5 exit criterion
criteria.notes: Assess both vertical (drop jump) and horizontal (bounding/hop) RSI. Both must show <10% asymmetry. RSI = jump height / ground contact time.

title: Load Progression Criteria in Exercise Programmes in Lower Limb Tendinopathy: A Systematic Review
authors: Escriche-Escuder A, Pinto-Carral A, Trinidad-Fernandez M, McAuliffe S, Fernandez-de-las-Penas C, Fuentes-Abolafio IJ, Roldán-Jiménez C, Cuesta-Vargas AI
summary: Systematic review classifying the types of load progression criteria used across exercise-based RCTs for lower limb tendinopathies including Achilles tendinopathy. Identifies six categories of progression criteria and their frequency of use. Concludes that pain-based criteria dominate clinical trials but highlights a critical evidence gap: there is limited evidence that pain-based progression criteria accurately reflect underlying physical capacity. This has direct implications for tendinopathy rehabilitation frameworks — symptom monitoring is necessary but not sufficient for progression decisions.
key_points: Six types of load progression criteria identified: (1) evoking pain-based, (2) avoid pain-based, (3) conditioning stages defined a priori, (4) fatigue-based, (5) subjective perception, (6) temporary linear increase
Pain-based criteria (types 1 and 2) are the most commonly used — present in the majority of included RCTs
Capacity-based criteria (objective performance tests) are used in a minority of trials
Critical evidence gap: pain-based criteria may not accurately reflect underlying tendon/neuromuscular capacity for progression
Systematic review published in BMJ Open — open access, high methodological rigour
Implications: progression frameworks should combine pain monitoring WITH capacity testing rather than relying on pain alone
Most studies did not measure performance outcomes — limits evidence for capacity-based progression
Fatigue-based progression (RPE, training to failure proximity) is evidence-supported for hypertrophy contexts
clinical_question: What types of progression criteria are used in lower limb tendinopathy exercise programs, and is there evidence that pain-based progression accurately reflects capacity?
applicability: Foundational for designing progression frameworks. Supports the hybrid approach: combine symptom monitoring (pain thresholds at multiple timepoints) with objective capacity testing (SLCR, hop tests, RSI asymmetry) rather than using pain as the sole progression gate.

recommended_loading_parameters.notes: Systematic review — not a loading protocol. Informs the criteria type to use: pain-based thresholds provide the primary gate (evidence base); capacity-based thresholds (SLCR, hop tests, RSI) provide secondary validation and are required for Stage 2→3 and return-to-sport decisions.

progression_criteria: Hybrid approach recommended: primary gate = pain-based thresholds (NPRS at multiple timepoints); secondary gate = objective capacity testing. Neither alone is sufficient for evidence-based progression decisions.
regression_criteria: Regression should be triggered by pain worsening (primary) and confirmed by capacity testing showing decline.
contraindications: N/A — systematic review.

title: Return to Sport in Athletes with Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy: A Qualitative Systematic Review on Prognostic Factors
authors: Habets B, van Cingel REH, Backx FJG, Huisstede BMA
source: Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine (PMC)
summary: Systematic review examining prognostic factors for successful return to sport in athletes with midportion Achilles tendinopathy. Identifies multi-factorial determinants across physical, psychological, and sport-specific domains. Key finding: return-to-sport planning should assess pain with activity plus recovery of tendon tissue, strength, ROM, function, and sport-specific demands; importantly, return-to-sport activity may begin before complete symptom resolution — supporting symptom-acceptability thresholds rather than zero-pain requirements.
key_points: Return to sport in Achilles tendinopathy is multi-factorial: pain, tendon tissue recovery, strength, ROM, function, and sport demands all contribute
Pain with activity is necessary to monitor but should not be the sole RTS criterion
